boundaries.evidence: The Definition's small-cases paragraph treats n=0 and the empty partition: x_emptyset=y_emptyset=z_emptyset=1, D_emptyset={1}, M(emptyset)=P(emptyset)=R with basis {1}, and the distinguished family is {x_emptyset}={1}.

The Definition requires q in R^x, including the unique unit of the zero ring, and it introduces every object by an explicit formula; it deliberately does not assert nondegeneracy of beta or of its restriction, so degenerate and zero form values lie inside the Definition's scope.
For n=1 the Definition records H=R with no generators, and for the one-box partition S_lambda=D_lambda={1}, M((1))=P((1))=R with beta(1,1)=q^0=1.

The Definition admits the extremal shapes uniformly: for (n) one has S_lambda=S_n, D_lambda={1}, and for (1^n) one has S_lambda={1}, D_lambda=S_n; t_lambda, w_lambda, x_lambda, y_lambda, z_lambda and the forms are defined for every partition with no nondegeneracy hypothesis.

The endpoints n=0 and n=1 are written into the Definition (for n=0,1 there are no generators and H=R), and the row blocks B_1,...,B_k are ordinary consecutive intervals, so the first and last indices carry no special hypothesis.
The Definition's final sentence records that no choice principle is used; the only distinguished selection, w_lambda, is unique by freeness and transitivity of the tableau action.

boundaries.reason: This is a Definition, not a biconditional theorem; existence and uniqueness of the star map, of w_lambda and of the minimal-length representatives in D_lambda are asserted outright.
No converse is claimed: the Definition does not assert that every anti-automorphism with T_i^*=T_i must be the reversal map.

citations.quote:
Let $n\ge0$ be an integer, with $S_0=\{1\}$ as in
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]. Let $A:=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ be the ring of Laurent polynomials in one
indeterminate $v$ over $\mathbb Z$. For $n\ge2$ the **generic type-A Hecke
algebra** $H_v(n)$ is the associative unital $A$-algebra presented by generators
$T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$ and the relations
$$T_i^2=(v-1)T_i+v\quad(1\le i<n),\qquad T_iT_{i+1}T_i=T_{i+1}T_iT_{i+1}\quad(1\le i\le n-2),\qquad T_iT_j=T_jT_i\quad(1\le i,j<n,\ |i-j|>1),$$
that is, the quotient of the free unital associative $A$-algebra on
$T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$ by the two-sided ideal generated by these relators. The
first relation is written in the **RG-13 quadratic normalization**
$(T_i-v)(T_i+1)=0$, equivalent to the displayed form over $A$. For $n\le1$ there
are no generators and we set $H_v(n):=A$.

**Standard basis elements.** Let $S_n=\operatorname{Sym}(\{1,\dots,n\})$ with
simple transpositions $s_i=(i\ i+1)$
([[def-symmetric-group]]), and let $w\in S_n$ have inversion length $\ell(w)=\ell$
([[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]). Choose a reduced expression
$w=s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_\ell}$, that is, a word of the minimal length $\ell(w)$
representing $w$, and put
$$T_w:=T_{i_1}\cdots T_{i_\ell}\in H_v(n),$$
the empty product when $w$ is the identity of $S_n$, so that $T_w=1$ for that
element. That $T_w$ is independent of the chosen reduced expression, and that
the elements $T_w$ form an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$, is proved in the
standard-basis theorem below
([[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]); the notation
distinguishes the generator $T_i$ with $1\le i\le n-1$ from $T_w$ for the group
element $w$.

**Specializations.** Let $R$ be a commutative $A$-algebra with structure map
$\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]\to R$, $v\mapsto v_0$, and suppose $v_0\in R^\times$. The
**specialization** of $H_v(n)$ at $v_0$ is the $R$-algebra
$R\otimes_AH_v(n)$; it is presented over $R$ by the images of $T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$
subject to the same relations with $v$ replaced by $v_0$, and we write $H_{v_0}(n)$
for it. Two specializations are used on this page: $v\mapsto1$, where the
quadratic relation becomes $T_i^2=1$ together with the braid and commutation
relations, and $v\mapsto q$, where $q$ is the prime power defining
$\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb F_q)$; the latter specializes the generic algebra to
the Hecke algebra attached to the finite general linear group. The condition
$v_0\in R^\times$ is part of the definition of a specialization and, for a nonzero coefficient ring $R$, excludes $v_0=0$. The zero ring
is allowed: its unique element is a unit and its specialization is the zero algebra.

In the generic type-A Hecke algebra $H_v(n)$ over $A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ with
generators $T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$, the quadratic relations
$(T_i-v)(T_i+1)=0$, the braid relations and the distant commutations, and with
$T_w$ the product of the $T_i$ along a reduced word for $w\in S_n$
([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]):

1. $\{T_w:w\in S_n\}$ is an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$; in particular $H_v(n)$ is
free of rank $n!$ over $A$;
2. for every $w\in S_n$ and every $1\le i\le n-1$,
$$T_wT_i=T_{ws_i}\quad\text{if }\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)+1,\qquad T_wT_i=(v-1)T_w+v\,T_{ws_i}\quad\text{if }\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)-1,$$
where $\ell$ is the inversion length of $S_n$
([[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]); consequently the rule rewrites
every monomial in the generators as an $A$-linear combination of the $T_w$.

No choice principle is used.

**Permutation matrices and the monomial subgroup.** Let $n\ge1$, let $q$ be a
prime power, let $G=\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb F_q)$ with diagonal torus $T$ and
standard flag $V_0\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq V_n$ as in
[[def-standard-subgroups-of-gl-n-over-a-finite-field]], and let
$S_n:=\operatorname{Sym}(\{1,\dots,n\})$ be the symmetric group of the set
$\{1,\dots,n\}$ ([[def-symmetric-group]], [[lem-symmetric-group-is-a-group]]),
so that permutations are composed as functions and an element $\sigma\in S_n$ is
written in one-line notation as the list $\sigma(1),\sigma(2),\dots,\sigma(n)$.

For $\sigma\in S_n$ the **permutation matrix** $P_\sigma\in G$ is the matrix with
$$(P_\sigma)_{ij}=\begin{cases}1,&i=\sigma(j),\\0,&i\ne\sigma(j),\end{cases}$$
that is, the $j$-th column of $P_\sigma$ is the standard basis vector
$e_{\sigma(j)}$, so that the $j$-th column has its unique entry $1$ in row
$\sigma(j)$. In particular $P_{\mathrm{id}}=I_n$, and multiplying matrices gives
$$P_\sigma P_\tau=P_{\sigma\circ\tau}\qquad(\sigma,\tau\in S_n),$$
because the $(i,k)$ entry of $P_\sigma P_\tau$ is $\sum_j(P_\sigma)_{ij}(P_\tau)_{jk}$,
which is $1$ exactly when $j=\tau(k)$ and $i=\sigma(j)=\sigma(\tau(k))$, and $0$
otherwise. A matrix $m\in G$ is **monomial** when every row and every column of
$m$ has exactly one nonzero entry. The **monomial subgroup** of $G$ is
$$N:=\{\,m\in G:m\text{ is monomial}\,\}.$$
Every $m\in N$ has a unique expression
$$m=t\,P_\sigma,\qquad t=\operatorname{diag}(t_1,\dots,t_n)\in T,\quad\sigma\in S_n,$$
namely with $\sigma(j)$ the row of the nonzero entry of column $j$ and
$t_{\sigma(j)}$ that entry; conversely $tP_\sigma$ is monomial with nonzero
entries $t_i$ in the rows and columns determined by $\sigma$. Consequently
$$N=T\cdot\{P_\sigma:\sigma\in S_n\}=\{P_\sigma t':\sigma\in S_n,\ t'\in T\},$$
since diagonal matrices may be moved across a permutation matrix.
$N$ is a subgroup of $G$: it contains $I_n=P_{\mathrm{id}}$, the product
$m m'$ of monomial matrices is monomial because the unique nonzero entry of each
column of $m'$ is transported to a unique nonzero entry of the corresponding
column of $mm'$, and the inverse of a monomial matrix is monomial since
permuting and rescaling rows and columns can be undone. Moreover $T\le N$ and
$T\mathrel{\trianglelefteq}N$.

**The Weyl group.** Define the **sign permutation** of a monomial matrix by
$$w:N\longrightarrow S_n,\qquad w(tP_\sigma):=\sigma,$$
which is well defined by the uniqueness of the decomposition. It is a group
homomorphism: if $m=tP_\sigma$ and $m'=t'P_\tau$, then
$t''':=P_\sigma t'P_\sigma^{-1}$ is diagonal, so
$mm'=t\,t'''\,P_\sigma P_\tau=t\,t'''\,P_{\sigma\tau}$ by
[[thm-matrix-multiplication-laws]], whence $w(mm')=\sigma\circ\tau=w(m)w(m')$.
Its kernel is exactly $T$, since $w(tP_\sigma)=\mathrm{id}$ says
$\sigma=\mathrm{id}$ and then $tP_{\mathrm{id}}=t$. Being a surjective
homomorphism, $w$ has kernel $T\mathrel{\trianglelefteq}N$ by
[[def-normal-subgroup]], and the induced map on cosets
$$W:=N/T\longrightarrow S_n,\qquad mT\longmapsto w(m),$$
is well defined (left multiplication by an element of $T=\ker w$ does not change
$w$) and is an isomorphism of groups, with inverse $\sigma\mapsto P_\sigma T$;
here $N/T$ is the quotient group of [[def-quotient-group]]. We call
$$W=N/T\cong S_n$$
the **(split) Weyl group** of $G$. Note that $W$ is defined as a quotient of the
monomial subgroup $N$ and **not** as the quotient $N_G(T)/T$ of the normaliser
of $T$ inside $G$: at $q=2$ the torus $T$ is trivial and $N_G(T)/T$ is all of
$G$, while $N/T\cong S_n$ still holds. For $\sigma\in S_n$ we write $w_\sigma$ for
the class of $P_\sigma$ in $W$, so that $w_\sigma w_\tau=w_{\sigma\tau}$ and the
isomorphism above sends $w_\sigma$ to $\sigma$; we write $1:=w_{\mathrm{id}}$
for the identity of $W$.

**Simple reflections.** For $1\le i<n$ let $s_i:=(i\ i+1)\in S_n$ be the
adjacent transposition of $i$ and $i+1$
([[def-symmetric-group]]), and put
$$\mathbf s_i:=w_{s_i}=P_{s_i}T\in W .$$
The elements $\mathbf s_1,\dots,\mathbf s_{n-1}$ are the **simple reflections** of
$W$; they generate $W$, because the adjacent transpositions generate $S_n$
([[thm-adjacent-transpositions-generate-the-symmetric-group]]) and $w$ is
surjective.

**Inversion length.** For $\sigma\in S_n$ the **inversion set** and **length**
are
$$\operatorname{Inv}(\sigma):=\{\,(i,j):1\le i<j\le n,\ \sigma(i)>\sigma(j)\,\}, \qquad \ell(\sigma):=\#\operatorname{Inv}(\sigma),$$
and for $w_\sigma\in W$ we set $\ell(w_\sigma):=\ell(\sigma)$, which is
well defined because every element of $W$ has the form $w_\sigma$ for exactly
one $\sigma$. Thus $\ell(1)=0$ and $\ell(w_{s_i})=1$ for every $i$, a single
inversion being created by the transposition of adjacent entries. Length is
invariant under inversion of the permutation: the map
$(i,j)\mapsto(\sigma(j),\sigma(i))$ is a bijection from $\operatorname{Inv}(\sigma)$
to $\operatorname{Inv}(\sigma^{-1})$ — if $i<j$ and $\sigma(i)>\sigma(j)$, then
setting $a:=\sigma(j)<b:=\sigma(i)$ gives $a<b$ while
$\sigma^{-1}(a)=j>i=\sigma^{-1}(b)$ — hence
$$\ell(w^{-1})=\ell(w)\qquad(w\in W).$$
We stress that $\ell$ is here defined combinatorially as an inversion count and
that no Coxeter-theoretic description of it as a minimal word length is used on
this page.

**Parabolic Weyl subgroups.** Let $\alpha=(a_1,\dots,a_r)$ be a composition of
$n$ with blocks $I_1,\dots,I_r$ and standard parabolic $P_\alpha$ and Levi
$L_\alpha$ ([[def-compositions-partial-flags-and-standard-parabolics]]). The
**standard parabolic subgroup of $W$** attached to $\alpha$ is
$$W_\alpha:=\{\,\sigma\in S_n:\sigma(I_i)=I_i\text{ for every }1\le i\le r\,\},$$
the group of permutations preserving each block of $\alpha$ as a set; it is
isomorphic to $S_{a_1}\times\cdots\times S_{a_r}$ by restriction to the blocks,
and its elements are exactly the $\sigma$ whose length is the sum of the lengths
of the restrictions $\sigma|_{I_i}$. In terms of the monomial subgroup, a
monomial matrix lies in $P_\alpha$ exactly when its permutation matrix has
$\sigma(I_i)=I_i$ for all $i$, that is, exactly when $\sigma\in W_\alpha$;
consequently
$$N\cap P_\alpha=N\cap L_\alpha=T\cdot\{\,P_\sigma:\sigma\in W_\alpha\,\}, \qquad W_\alpha=w(N\cap P_\alpha),$$
and $\{P_\sigma:\sigma\in W_\alpha\}$ is a complement to $T$ in $N\cap P_\alpha$: its intersection with $T$ is $\{I_n\}$ and every element has the unique form $tP_\sigma$. The two extreme
cases are
$$W_{(n)}=S_n,\qquad W_{(1^n)}=\{1\},$$
corresponding to $P_{(n)}=G=L_{(n)}$ and to $P_{(1^n)}=B$ with $L_{(1^n)}=T$
and $W_{(1^n)}=w(T)=\{1\}$: the single block of $(n)$ is preserved by every
permutation, while each singleton block of $(1^n)$ must be fixed, so only the
identity survives.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $q\in R^\times$, let $n\ge0$, and let
$H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$ be the type-A Hecke algebra over $R$ with generators
$T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$, quadratic relations $(T_i-q)(T_i+1)=0$, braid and distant
commutation relations, and standard basis $\{T_w:w\in S_n\}$
([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]],
[[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]); here
$\ell(w)$ is the inversion length of $w\in S_n$
([[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]). All modules below are right
modules.

**The star anti-involution.** Let $\sigma\mapsto\sigma^*$ be the unique
$R$-algebra anti-automorphism of $H$ with $T_i^*=T_i$ for every generator: it
exists because reversal of words preserves the ideal of defining relations
(the quadratic and braid relators are fixed, while a distant commutation relator is sent to its negative), so reversal descends from the free algebra to $H$, and it is
unique because the generators generate $H$. On the standard basis
$T_w^*=T_{w^{-1}}$, since reversing a reduced word for $w$ is a reduced word
for $w^{-1}$.

**Tableau conventions.** Write $t\cdot\sigma$ for the right action of $S_n$ on
tableaux defined by $(t\cdot\sigma)(c):=\sigma^{-1}(t(c))$; it is the inverse
of the left action $(\sigma\cdot t)(c)=\sigma(t(c))$ of
[[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]], and it is a right action.
A $\lambda$-tableau is **row standard** when its entries strictly increase
along every row; columns are not constrained. Let $t^\lambda$ be the row-filled
$\lambda$-tableau, whose row $i$ carries
$\lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_{i-1}+1,\dots,\lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_i$ from left
to right, and let $t_\lambda$ be the column-filled $\lambda$-tableau, whose
column $j$ carries consecutive integers downward; equivalently
$t_\lambda(i,j)=t^{\lambda'}(j,i)$, so that $t_\lambda$ is the transpose of
$t^{\lambda'}$ ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]).

**The row subgroup and the coset representatives.** Let $S_\lambda$ be the
**row subgroup** of $\lambda$, the subgroup of $S_n$ preserving every row of
$t^\lambda$; writing
$$B_i:=\{\lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_{i-1}+1,\ \lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_{i-1}+2,\ \dots,\ \lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_i\}$$
for the $i$-th row block of $t^\lambda$, one has
$S_\lambda=S(B_1)\times\cdots\times S(B_k)$, the direct product of the
symmetric groups of the individual row blocks. Let
$$D_\lambda:=\{d\in S_n:t^\lambda\cdot d\text{ is row standard}\}.$$
This is the set of minimal-length right coset representatives of $S_\lambda$ in
$S_n$: every right coset $S_\lambda d$ has exactly one element $d_0$ for which
$t^\lambda\cdot d_0$ is row standard, and it satisfies
$\ell(wd_0)=\ell(w)+\ell(d_0)$ for all $w\in S_\lambda$
([[lem-dj-bridge-row-permutation-module-standard-action]]). Let
$w_\lambda\in S_n$ be the unique element with $t^\lambda\cdot w_\lambda=t_\lambda$;
existence and uniqueness hold because the action of $S_n$ on $\lambda$-tableaux
is free and transitive.

**Generators and modules.** For a partition $\lambda\vdash n$ put
$$x_\lambda:=\sum_{w\in S_\lambda}T_w,\qquad y_\lambda:=\sum_{w\in S_\lambda}(-q)^{-\ell(w)}T_w,\qquad z_\lambda:=x_\lambda T_{w_\lambda}y_{\lambda'},$$
where $\lambda'$ is the conjugate partition of $\lambda$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). The **row
permutation module** is the right ideal $M(\lambda):=x_\lambda H\subseteq H$,
and the **ordinary Dipper-James polytabloid module** is
$P(\lambda):=z_\lambda H\subseteq M(\lambda)$; $z_\lambda$ is its polytabloid
generator.

**The forms.** The **permutation form** is the $R$-bilinear form $\beta$ on
$M(\lambda)$ determined on the distinguished family
$\{x_\lambda T_d:d\in D_\lambda\}$ by
$$\beta(x_\lambda T_d,x_\lambda T_e)=\delta_{d,e}q^{\ell(d)}\qquad(d,e\in D_\lambda),$$
and the **DJ form** is the restriction of $\beta$ to $P(\lambda)$. That family
is an $R$-basis of $M(\lambda)$
([[lem-dj-bridge-row-permutation-module-standard-action]]), so the displayed
values define a unique bilinear form; the family is $\{x_\varnothing\}=\{1\}$
for the empty partition.

**Small cases and base change.** For $\lambda=\varnothing$ set
$x_\varnothing=y_\varnothing=z_\varnothing=1$, so that
$M(\varnothing)=P(\varnothing)=R$ and $\beta$ is the standard form; for
$n=0,1$ there are no generators and $H=R$. Every base change
$A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]\to R$, $v\mapsto q$, with $q\in R^\times$, produces all
objects above over $R$ by the same formulas; the suppliers of this page prove
that the distinguished families and the form are compatible with such base
change. No choice principle is used.

Let $\lambda\vdash n$ and let $[\lambda]$ be its Young diagram
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). A **tableau of shape
$\lambda$**, or $\lambda$-tableau, is a bijection
$$t:[\lambda]\longrightarrow\{1,2,\dots,n\}.$$
We write $t(i,j)$ for the entry of $t$ in the node $(i,j)$, and we display $t$
as the diagram $[\lambda]$ with each node carrying its entry. Thus a tableau
places each of the numbers $1,\dots,n$ in exactly one node of $[\lambda]$. For
$\lambda=\varnothing$ the diagram is empty and the empty map is the unique
tableau of shape $\varnothing$, the **empty tableau**. The **shape** of a
tableau $t$ is the partition $\lambda$ with $t:[\lambda]\to\{1,\dots,n\}$,
which is determined by $t$ because $[\lambda]$ determines $\lambda$.

**Standard tableaux.** A tableau $t$ of shape $\lambda$ is **standard** if its
entries strictly increase along rows and down columns, that is, if
$$t(i,j)<t(i,j+1)\quad\text{whenever }(i,j),(i,j+1)\in[\lambda],$$
$$t(i,j)<t(i+1,j)\quad\text{whenever }(i,j),(i+1,j)\in[\lambda].$$
The empty tableau is standard, because both conditions are vacuous, and it is
the unique standard tableau of shape $\varnothing$. Following the classical
notation we write $f^\lambda$ for the number of standard $\lambda$-tableaux.

**The left action on tableaux.** For $\sigma\in S_n$ and a $\lambda$-tableau
$t$, define
$$(\sigma\cdot t)(i,j):=\sigma\bigl(t(i,j)\bigr)\qquad\bigl((i,j)\in[\lambda]\bigr).$$
Since $t$ is a bijection onto $\{1,\dots,n\}$ and $\sigma$ is a bijection of
$\{1,\dots,n\}$, the map $\sigma\cdot t$ is again a bijection
$[\lambda]\to\{1,\dots,n\}$, hence again a $\lambda$-tableau, and
$\mathrm{id}\cdot t=t$, $\sigma\cdot(\tau\cdot t)=(\sigma\tau)\cdot t$ for all
$\sigma,\tau\in S_n$: the rule is a left action of $S_n$ on the set of
$\lambda$-tableaux. For every $\sigma\in S_n$ the row sets of $\sigma\cdot t$
are the images under $\sigma$ of the row sets of $t$, and the column sets of
$\sigma\cdot t$ are the images under $\sigma$ of the column sets of $t$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $q\in R^\times$, let $n\ge0$, and let
$H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$ be the type-A Hecke algebra over $R$ with generators
$T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$, quadratic relations $(T_i-q)(T_i+1)=0$, braid and distant
commutation relations, and standard basis $\{T_w:w\in S_n\}$
([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]],
[[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]); here
$\ell(w)$ is the inversion length of $w\in S_n$
([[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]). All modules below are right
modules.

$R$-algebra anti-automorphism of $H$ with $T_i^*=T_i$ for every generator: it
exists because reversal of words preserves the ideal of defining relations
(the quadratic and braid relators are fixed, while a distant commutation relator is sent to its negative), so reversal descends from the free algebra to $H$, and it is
unique because the generators generate $H$. On the standard basis

for $w^{-1}$.

of the left action $(\sigma\cdot t)(c)=\sigma(t(c))$ of
[[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]], and it is a right action.
A $\lambda$-tableau is **row standard** when its entries strictly increase

$\lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_{i-1}+1,\dots,\lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_i$ from left
to right, and let $t_\lambda$ be the column-filled $\lambda$-tableau, whose
column $j$ carries consecutive integers downward; equivalently
$t_\lambda(i,j)=t^{\lambda'}(j,i)$, so that $t_\lambda$ is the transpose of
$t^{\lambda'}$ ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]).

**The row subgroup and the coset representatives.** Let $S_\lambda$ be the
**row subgroup** of $\lambda$, the subgroup of $S_n$ preserving every row of
$t^\lambda$; writing
$$B_i:=\{\lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_{i-1}+1,\ \lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_{i-1}+2,\ \dots,\ \lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_i\}$$
for the $i$-th row block of $t^\lambda$, one has
$S_\lambda=S(B_1)\times\cdots\times S(B_k)$, the direct product of the
symmetric groups of the individual row blocks. Let
$$D_\lambda:=\{d\in S_n:t^\lambda\cdot d\text{ is row standard}\}.$$
This is the set of minimal-length right coset representatives of $S_\lambda$ in
$S_n$: every right coset $S_\lambda d$ has exactly one element $d_0$ for which
$t^\lambda\cdot d_0$ is row standard, and it satisfies
$\ell(wd_0)=\ell(w)+\ell(d_0)$ for all $w\in S_\lambda$
([[lem-dj-bridge-row-permutation-module-standard-action]]). Let
$w_\lambda\in S_n$ be the unique element with $t^\lambda\cdot w_\lambda=t_\lambda$;
existence and uniqueness hold because the action of $S_n$ on $\lambda$-tableaux
is free and transitive.

$$x_\lambda:=\sum_{w\in S_\lambda}T_w,\qquad y_\lambda:=\sum_{w\in S_\lambda}(-q)^{-\ell(w)}T_w,\qquad z_\lambda:=x_\lambda T_{w_\lambda}y_{\lambda'},$$
where $\lambda'$ is the conjugate partition of $\lambda$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). The **row
permutation module** is the right ideal $M(\lambda):=x_\lambda H\subseteq H$,
and the **ordinary Dipper-James polytabloid module** is
$P(\lambda):=z_\lambda H\subseteq M(\lambda)$; $z_\lambda$ is its polytabloid
generator.

**The forms.** The **permutation form** is the $R$-bilinear form $\beta$ on
$M(\lambda)$ determined on the distinguished family
$\{x_\lambda T_d:d\in D_\lambda\}$ by
$$\beta(x_\lambda T_d,x_\lambda T_e)=\delta_{d,e}q^{\ell(d)}\qquad(d,e\in D_\lambda),$$
and the **DJ form** is the restriction of $\beta$ to $P(\lambda)$. That family
is an $R$-basis of $M(\lambda)$
([[lem-dj-bridge-row-permutation-module-standard-action]]), so the displayed
values define a unique bilinear form; the family is $\{x_\varnothing\}=\{1\}$
for the empty partition.

**Small cases and base change.** For $\lambda=\varnothing$ set
$x_\varnothing=y_\varnothing=z_\varnothing=1$, so that
$M(\varnothing)=P(\varnothing)=R$ and $\beta$ is the standard form; for
$n=0,1$ there are no generators and $H=R$. Every base change
$A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]\to R$, $v\mapsto q$, with $q\in R^\times$, produces all
objects above over $R$ by the same formulas; the suppliers of this page prove
that the distinguished families and the form are compatible with such base
change. No choice principle is used.

derivations.claim: **Length and multiplication criteria for one generator.** Let $g\in S_n$ and $1\le i<n$. The one-line list of $gs_i$ is obtained from that of $g$ by exchanging the entries $g(i),g(i+1)$ at positions $i,i+1$, and only the relative order of this single pair changes, so $\ell(gs_i)=\ell(g)+1$ if $g(i)<g(i+1)$ and $\ell(gs_i)=\ell(g)-1$ if $g(i)>g(i+1)$. Replacing $g$ by $g^{-1}$ gives $\ell(s_ig)=\ell(g^{-1}s_i)$ equal to $\ell(g)+1$ if and only if $g^{-1}(i)<g^{-1}(i+1)$. Thus [F1] gives $T_gT_i=T_{gs_i}$ under the right ascent hypothesis $g(i)<g(i+1)$; under the left ascent hypothesis $g^{-1}(i)<g^{-1}(i+1)$, applying [F1] to $g^{-1}$ and then $*$ gives $T_iT_g=T_{s_ig}$.

**Order preservation inside rows.** If $d\in D_\lambda$ and $a<b$ are entries lying in the same row of $t^\lambda$, then $d^{-1}(a)<d^{-1}(b)$. Indeed the boxes of $a$ and $b$ lie in that row with the box of $a$ to the left, and $t^\lambda\cdot d=d^{-1}\cdot t^\lambda$ carries those boxes to the entries $d^{-1}(a),d^{-1}(b)$; since $t^\lambda\cdot d$ is row standard, its entries increase along the row.

**The coset representatives.** The row sets of $t^\lambda\cdot g$ are $g^{-1}(B_1),\dots,g^{-1}(B_k)$ by [F4], so $t^\lambda\cdot g$ and $t^\lambda\cdot g'$ have the same row sets if and only if $g'g^{-1}$ preserves every $B_r$, that is, if and only if $g'\in S_\lambda g$. For a given right coset $S_\lambda g$, the tableau $t^\lambda\cdot g$ has some row sets; filling each row by its entries in increasing order gives a row-standard tableau with the same row sets, and it equals $t^\lambda\cdot y$ for some $y\in S_n$ because the action of $S_n$ on tableaux is transitive. That $y$ lies in $S_\lambda g$, since it has the same row sets as $t^\lambda\cdot g$. Two row-standard tableaux with the same row sets are equal, and the action on tableaux is free, so $y$ is unique in its coset; hence $D_\lambda$ is a complete set of right coset representatives of $S_\lambda$ in $S_n$.

**The parabolic identities.** For every $w\in S_\lambda$ one has $x_\lambda T_w=q^{\ell(w)}x_\lambda$, $T_wx_\lambda=q^{\ell(w)}x_\lambda$ and $x_\lambda^*=x_\lambda$. For a generator $s_i\in S_\lambda$ split $S_\lambda$ into $A=\{u:\ell(us_i)>\ell(u)\}$ and its complement $B$; right multiplication by $s_i$ bijects $A$ onto $B$, and the multiplication rule gives $$x_\lambda T_i=\sum_{u\in A}T_{us_i}+\sum_{u\in B}\bigl((q-1)T_u+qT_{us_i}\bigr)=\sum_{v\in B}T_v+(q-1)\sum_{u\in B}T_u+q\sum_{v\in A}T_v=q\,x_\lambda.$$ Since every product $us_i$ with $u\in S_\lambda$ lies in $S_\lambda$, induction on $\ell(w)=\ell(vs_i)=\ell(v)+1$ gives $x_\lambda T_w=(x_\lambda T_v)T_i=q^{\ell(v)}q\,x_\lambda=q^{\ell(w)}x_\lambda$. The star map sends each $T_w$ to $T_{w^{-1}}$ and permutes the sum $x_\lambda$, so $x_\lambda^*=x_\lambda$; then $(T_wx_\lambda)^*=x_\lambda T_{w^{-1}}=q^{\ell(w^{-1})}x_\lambda=q^{\ell(w)}x_\lambda$ by [F2], and applying $*$ again gives $T_wx_\lambda=q^{\ell(w)}x_\lambda$.

**Length additivity and multiplicativity.** For $w\in S_\lambda$ and $d\in D_\lambda$ one has $\ell(wd)=\ell(w)+\ell(d)$ and $T_wT_d=T_{wd}$. Prove this by induction on $\ell(w)$. For $w=1$ both claims are immediate. For $\ell(w)\ge1$ write $w=s_iv$ with $s_i\in S_\lambda$ a simple reflection of $S_\lambda$ and $\ell(w)=1+\ell(v)$; then $\ell(s_iv)=\ell(v)+1$, so $v^{-1}(i)<v^{-1}(i+1)$ by step 1.1. Because $s_i\in S_\lambda$, the labels $i,i+1$ lie in one row block $B_r$, and $v^{-1}\in S_\lambda$ preserves every row block, so $v^{-1}(i)$ and $v^{-1}(i+1)$ lie in the same row of $t^\lambda$; step 1.2 then gives $(vd)^{-1}(i)=d^{-1}(v^{-1}(i))<d^{-1}(v^{-1}(i+1))=(vd)^{-1}(i+1)$, whence $\ell(s_ivd)=\ell(vd)+1$ by step 1.1. The induction hypothesis gives $\ell(vd)=\ell(v)+\ell(d)$, so $\ell(wd)=\ell(s_ivd)=\ell(v)+1+\ell(d)=\ell(w)+\ell(d)$. For the basis elements, step 1.1 gives $T_{s_i}T_{vd}=T_{s_ivd}$ since $\ell(s_ivd)=\ell(vd)+1$, so $T_wT_d=T_{s_i}(T_vT_d)=T_{s_i}T_{vd}=T_{wd}$ using the induction hypothesis $T_vT_d=T_{vd}$.

**The shape of the three cases.** Let $d\in D_\lambda$, $t=t^\lambda\cdot d$, $s=t\cdot s_i=s_i\cdot t=t^\lambda\cdot(ds_i)$. First, $s$ is row standard if and only if $i$ and $i+1$ lie in different rows of $t$: if they lie in the same row then $i$ is left of $i+1$ and the swap creates a descent in that row, while if they lie in different rows then each affected row keeps the same two neighbours of the moved entry, the left neighbour smaller than $i$ and the right neighbour larger than $i+1$, so both inequalities persist. Second, the position of a label $j$ in the row-reading word of $t$ equals $d(j)$, because $t=d^{-1}\cdot t^\lambda$; so by step 1.1, $\ell(ds_i)=\ell(d)+1$ holds exactly when $i$ precedes $i+1$ in $t$, and this happens in particular when $i$ and $i+1$ lie in the same row.

**The basis.** For $d\in D_\lambda$, step 2.1 gives $x_\lambda T_d=\sum_{w\in S_\lambda}T_wT_d=\sum_{w\in S_\lambda}T_{wd}$, whose support in the standard basis is exactly the right coset $S_\lambda d$ with coefficient $1$ at every element. By step 1.3 the cosets $S_\lambda d$, $d\in D_\lambda$, are pairwise disjoint and partition $S_n$, so the supports of the $x_\lambda T_d$ are disjoint; since the $T_w$ are $R$-linearly independent by [F1], the family $\{x_\lambda T_d:d\in D_\lambda\}$ is linearly independent. For an arbitrary $g\in S_n$, step 1.3 lets us write $g=wd$ with $w\in S_\lambda$, $d\in D_\lambda$, and then $x_\lambda T_g=x_\lambda T_wT_d=q^{\ell(w)}x_\lambda T_d$ by steps 2.1 and 1.4; since the $T_g$ span $H$ by [F1], the family spans the right ideal $M(\lambda)=x_\lambda H$. Hence it is a basis and $M(\lambda)$ is free, which is clause (1).

**Case of one row.** Suppose $i$ and $i+1$ lie in the same row of $t$. Then $s$ has the same row sets as $t$, so $ds_i$ and $d$ lie in the same right coset of $S_\lambda$ by step 1.3, say $ds_i=wd$ with $w\in S_\lambda$. By steps 2.1 and 2.2, $\ell(d)+1=\ell(ds_i)=\ell(wd)=\ell(w)+\ell(d)$, so $\ell(w)=1$. The multiplication rule [F1] and step 2.2 give $x_\lambda T_dT_i=x_\lambda T_{ds_i}=x_\lambda T_{wd}=x_\lambda T_wT_d=q^{\ell(w)}x_\lambda T_d=q\,x_\lambda T_d$, using step 1.4. This is the first displayed case.

**Case of two rows.** Suppose $i$ and $i+1$ lie in different rows of $t$. Then $s$ is row standard by step 2.2, so $d':=ds_i$ lies in $D_\lambda$ and $t^\lambda\cdot d'=s$; this is the element $d'$ of the statement. The multiplication rule [F1] gives $x_\lambda T_dT_i=x_\lambda T_{d'}$ if $\ell(d')=\ell(d)+1$, and $x_\lambda T_dT_i=(q-1)x_\lambda T_d+q\,x_\lambda T_{d'}$ if $\ell(d')=\ell(d)-1$. These are the second and third displayed cases, and together with step 3.2 they prove clause (3).

**Base change.** All constructions above are defined over an arbitrary commutative $R$ with $q\in R^\times$ by the formulas of [[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]], and every identity was obtained from the presentation and from inversion counts, so its coefficients are Laurent polynomials in $q$ with integer coefficients. Given a ring map $R\to R'$ with $q\mapsto q'\in(R')^\times$, the base change sends $H_{R,q}(S_n)$ to $H_{R',q'}(S_n)$ and the elements $T_w$, $x_\lambda$ to their images $T'_w$, $x'_\lambda$; the basis $\{x_\lambda T_d\}$ maps to the corresponding basis, and the formulas of steps 1.4, 2.1 and 3.1 specialize termwise, so clause (4) follows.

Clauses (1), (2), (3) and (4) are established by steps 3.1, 1.4, 3.2, 4.1 and 4.2. Only inversion counts, the presentation of $H$, the structure of the row groups and the standard basis are used; no choice principle is used.

Star sends T_w to T_(w inverse), never to the algebra inverse. Empty/one-box/zero ring and all base changes retain the formulas. Mathas Lemma 3.2, Proposition 3.3 and Corollary 3.4 read in full.

boundaries.evidence: Step 1.1 treats lambda=emptyset explicitly: the basis is {1} and beta(1,1)=q^0=1; steps 1.2-2.1 are vacuous because there are no generators, and step 4.1 specializes the rank-one matrix (1) of weights.

The zero ring is allowed; q in R^x excludes q=0 only when R is nonzero; beta is diagonal with unit weights q^{ell(d)} in the basis of step 1.1 and no step divides by q-1, so q=1 is allowed and the ambient form is unimodular (it is the zero pairing over the zero ring).

n=1: the one-box module has the single basis vector with beta(x_(1),x_(1))=1; there are no generators, so the induction of step 3.1 is the empty word and h=h^*=1; P((1))=M((1)) and the DJ form is the permutation form.

Single row lambda=(n): D_lambda={1}, the set S of step 1.2 is all of D_lambda and the self-adjointness check of step 2.1 is beta(x T_i,y)=q beta(x,y)=beta(x,y T_i); single column lambda=(1^n): step 1.2 partitions D_lambda=S_n into two-element orbits and the four pairings of step 2.1 cover the whole basis.

The orbit pairings of step 2.1 are verified at both ends u and v of each orbit, the induction of step 3.1 starts from the empty word, and the extreme data lambda=emptyset and the longest representative in D_lambda are covered by steps 1.1-1.2.
Step 5.1 records that no choice principle is used; beta is fixed by a formula on the fixed basis of step 1.1 and the orbit partition of step 1.2 is determined by the fixed index i.

boundaries.reason: The Statement asserts well-definedness, symmetry, contravariance and base change outright; the only equivalence-shaped claim, the orbit classification of step 1.2, is a dichotomy proved inside that step.
No converse is asserted; in particular the Statement does not claim that every contravariant form on M(lambda) equals the permutation form.

citations.quote:
In the notation of
[[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]], for every
commutative ring $R$ and every $q\in R^\times$:

1. $M(\lambda)$ is free with basis $\{x_\lambda T_d:d\in D_\lambda\}$;

2. $x_\lambda T_w=q^{\ell(w)}x_\lambda$ and $T_wx_\lambda=q^{\ell(w)}x_\lambda$
for every $w\in S_\lambda$, and $x_\lambda^*=x_\lambda$;

3. if $d\in D_\lambda$, $t=t^\lambda\cdot d$ and $s=t\cdot s_i=t^\lambda\cdot d'$, then
$$x_\lambda T_dT_i=\begin{cases}q\,x_\lambda T_d,&s\text{ is not row standard},\\ x_\lambda T_{d'},&s\text{ is row standard and }\ell(d')>\ell(d),\\ q\,x_\lambda T_{d'}+(q-1)x_\lambda T_d,&s\text{ is row standard and }\ell(d')<\ell(d);\end{cases}$$

4. the basis and the action formulas are compatible with every base change
$R\to R'$ along a ring map sending $q$ to a unit.

No choice principle is used.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $q\in R^\times$, let $n\ge0$, and let
$H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$ be the type-A Hecke algebra over $R$ with generators
$T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$, quadratic relations $(T_i-q)(T_i+1)=0$, braid and distant
commutation relations, and standard basis $\{T_w:w\in S_n\}$
([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]],
[[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]); here
$\ell(w)$ is the inversion length of $w\in S_n$
([[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]). All modules below are right
modules.

**The star anti-involution.** Let $\sigma\mapsto\sigma^*$ be the unique
$R$-algebra anti-automorphism of $H$ with $T_i^*=T_i$ for every generator: it
exists because reversal of words preserves the ideal of defining relations
(the quadratic and braid relators are fixed, while a distant commutation relator is sent to its negative), so reversal descends from the free algebra to $H$, and it is
unique because the generators generate $H$. On the standard basis
$T_w^*=T_{w^{-1}}$, since reversing a reduced word for $w$ is a reduced word
for $w^{-1}$.

**Tableau conventions.** Write $t\cdot\sigma$ for the right action of $S_n$ on
tableaux defined by $(t\cdot\sigma)(c):=\sigma^{-1}(t(c))$; it is the inverse
of the left action $(\sigma\cdot t)(c)=\sigma(t(c))$ of
[[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]], and it is a right action.
A $\lambda$-tableau is **row standard** when its entries strictly increase
along every row; columns are not constrained. Let $t^\lambda$ be the row-filled
$\lambda$-tableau, whose row $i$ carries
$\lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_{i-1}+1,\dots,\lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_i$ from left
to right, and let $t_\lambda$ be the column-filled $\lambda$-tableau, whose
column $j$ carries consecutive integers downward; equivalently
$t_\lambda(i,j)=t^{\lambda'}(j,i)$, so that $t_\lambda$ is the transpose of
$t^{\lambda'}$ ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]).

**The row subgroup and the coset representatives.** Let $S_\lambda$ be the
**row subgroup** of $\lambda$, the subgroup of $S_n$ preserving every row of
$t^\lambda$; writing
$$B_i:=\{\lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_{i-1}+1,\ \lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_{i-1}+2,\ \dots,\ \lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_i\}$$
for the $i$-th row block of $t^\lambda$, one has
$S_\lambda=S(B_1)\times\cdots\times S(B_k)$, the direct product of the
symmetric groups of the individual row blocks. Let
$$D_\lambda:=\{d\in S_n:t^\lambda\cdot d\text{ is row standard}\}.$$
This is the set of minimal-length right coset representatives of $S_\lambda$ in
$S_n$: every right coset $S_\lambda d$ has exactly one element $d_0$ for which
$t^\lambda\cdot d_0$ is row standard, and it satisfies
$\ell(wd_0)=\ell(w)+\ell(d_0)$ for all $w\in S_\lambda$
([[lem-dj-bridge-row-permutation-module-standard-action]]). Let
$w_\lambda\in S_n$ be the unique element with $t^\lambda\cdot w_\lambda=t_\lambda$;
existence and uniqueness hold because the action of $S_n$ on $\lambda$-tableaux
is free and transitive.

**Generators and modules.** For a partition $\lambda\vdash n$ put
$$x_\lambda:=\sum_{w\in S_\lambda}T_w,\qquad y_\lambda:=\sum_{w\in S_\lambda}(-q)^{-\ell(w)}T_w,\qquad z_\lambda:=x_\lambda T_{w_\lambda}y_{\lambda'},$$
where $\lambda'$ is the conjugate partition of $\lambda$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). The **row
permutation module** is the right ideal $M(\lambda):=x_\lambda H\subseteq H$,
and the **ordinary Dipper-James polytabloid module** is
$P(\lambda):=z_\lambda H\subseteq M(\lambda)$; $z_\lambda$ is its polytabloid
generator.

**The forms.** The **permutation form** is the $R$-bilinear form $\beta$ on
$M(\lambda)$ determined on the distinguished family
$\{x_\lambda T_d:d\in D_\lambda\}$ by
$$\beta(x_\lambda T_d,x_\lambda T_e)=\delta_{d,e}q^{\ell(d)}\qquad(d,e\in D_\lambda),$$
and the **DJ form** is the restriction of $\beta$ to $P(\lambda)$. That family
is an $R$-basis of $M(\lambda)$
([[lem-dj-bridge-row-permutation-module-standard-action]]), so the displayed
values define a unique bilinear form; the family is $\{x_\varnothing\}=\{1\}$
for the empty partition.

**Small cases and base change.** For $\lambda=\varnothing$ set
$x_\varnothing=y_\varnothing=z_\varnothing=1$, so that
$M(\varnothing)=P(\varnothing)=R$ and $\beta$ is the standard form; for
$n=0,1$ there are no generators and $H=R$. Every base change
$A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]\to R$, $v\mapsto q$, with $q\in R^\times$, produces all
objects above over $R$ by the same formulas; the suppliers of this page prove
that the distinguished families and the form are compatible with such base
change. No choice principle is used.

Let $n\ge0$ be an integer, with $S_0=\{1\}$ as in
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]. Let $A:=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ be the ring of Laurent polynomials in one
indeterminate $v$ over $\mathbb Z$. For $n\ge2$ the **generic type-A Hecke
algebra** $H_v(n)$ is the associative unital $A$-algebra presented by generators
$T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$ and the relations
$$T_i^2=(v-1)T_i+v\quad(1\le i<n),\qquad T_iT_{i+1}T_i=T_{i+1}T_iT_{i+1}\quad(1\le i\le n-2),\qquad T_iT_j=T_jT_i\quad(1\le i,j<n,\ |i-j|>1),$$
that is, the quotient of the free unital associative $A$-algebra on
$T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$ by the two-sided ideal generated by these relators. The
first relation is written in the **RG-13 quadratic normalization**
$(T_i-v)(T_i+1)=0$, equivalent to the displayed form over $A$. For $n\le1$ there
are no generators and we set $H_v(n):=A$.

**Standard basis elements.** Let $S_n=\operatorname{Sym}(\{1,\dots,n\})$ with
simple transpositions $s_i=(i\ i+1)$
([[def-symmetric-group]]), and let $w\in S_n$ have inversion length $\ell(w)=\ell$
([[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]). Choose a reduced expression
$w=s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_\ell}$, that is, a word of the minimal length $\ell(w)$
representing $w$, and put
$$T_w:=T_{i_1}\cdots T_{i_\ell}\in H_v(n),$$
the empty product when $w$ is the identity of $S_n$, so that $T_w=1$ for that
element. That $T_w$ is independent of the chosen reduced expression, and that
the elements $T_w$ form an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$, is proved in the
standard-basis theorem below
([[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]); the notation
distinguishes the generator $T_i$ with $1\le i\le n-1$ from $T_w$ for the group
element $w$.

**Specializations.** Let $R$ be a commutative $A$-algebra with structure map
$\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]\to R$, $v\mapsto v_0$, and suppose $v_0\in R^\times$. The
**specialization** of $H_v(n)$ at $v_0$ is the $R$-algebra
$R\otimes_AH_v(n)$; it is presented over $R$ by the images of $T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$
subject to the same relations with $v$ replaced by $v_0$, and we write $H_{v_0}(n)$
for it. Two specializations are used on this page: $v\mapsto1$, where the
quadratic relation becomes $T_i^2=1$ together with the braid and commutation
relations, and $v\mapsto q$, where $q$ is the prime power defining
$\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb F_q)$; the latter specializes the generic algebra to
the Hecke algebra attached to the finite general linear group. The condition
$v_0\in R^\times$ is part of the definition of a specialization and, for a nonzero coefficient ring $R$, excludes $v_0=0$. The zero ring
is allowed: its unique element is a unit and its specialization is the zero algebra.

and the **ordinary Dipper-James polytabloid module** is
$P(\lambda):=z_\lambda H\subseteq M(\lambda)$; $z_\lambda$ is its polytabloid
generator.

**The forms.** The **permutation form** is the $R$-bilinear form $\beta$ on
$M(\lambda)$ determined on the distinguished family
$\{x_\lambda T_d:d\in D_\lambda\}$ by
$$\beta(x_\lambda T_d,x_\lambda T_e)=\delta_{d,e}q^{\ell(d)}\qquad(d,e\in D_\lambda),$$
and the **DJ form** is the restriction of $\beta$ to $P(\lambda)$. That family
is an $R$-basis of $M(\lambda)$
([[lem-dj-bridge-row-permutation-module-standard-action]]), so the displayed
values define a unique bilinear form; the family is $\{x_\varnothing\}=\{1\}$
for the empty partition.

**Small cases and base change.** For $\lambda=\varnothing$ set
$x_\varnothing=y_\varnothing=z_\varnothing=1$, so that
$M(\varnothing)=P(\varnothing)=R$ and $\beta$ is the standard form; for
$n=0,1$ there are no generators and $H=R$. Every base change
$A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]\to R$, $v\mapsto q$, with $q\in R^\times$, produces all
objects above over $R$ by the same formulas; the suppliers of this page prove
that the distinguished families and the form are compatible with such base
change. No choice principle is used.

derivations.claim: **The form is well defined, symmetric and bilinear.** By [F1] the family $\{x_d:d\in D_\lambda\}$ is an $R$-basis of $M(\lambda)$, so there is exactly one $R$-bilinear form $\beta$ on $M(\lambda)$ whose Gram matrix in this basis is the diagonal matrix with entries $q^{\ell(d)}$, $d\in D_\lambda$; this form is symmetric because its Gram matrix is diagonal, and it is the permutation form of the statement. For $\lambda=\varnothing$ the basis is $\{1\}$ and $\beta(1,1)=q^0=1$.

**Orbits of one generator.** Fix $i$ and abbreviate $x_d:=x_\lambda T_d$. Partition $D_\lambda$ into the set $S$ of those $d$ for which $i,i+1$ lie in the same row of $t^\lambda\cdot d$, and the remaining set $D$; for $d\in D$ the element $d^*:=ds_i$ again lies in $D_\lambda$ and $(d^*)^*=d$, by the second and third cases of [F1] applied twice. Thus $D$ is partitioned into two-element orbits $\{u,v\}$ with $v=us_i$ and $\ell(v)=\ell(u)+1$, and the action on such an orbit is $x_uT_i=x_v$, $x_vT_i=qx_u+(q-1)x_v$, while $x_dT_i=qx_d$ for $d\in S$. In particular each $x_dT_i$ lies in the span of the orbit of $d$.

**Self-adjointness of the generators.** In an orbit $\{u,v\}$ with $\ell(v)=\ell(u)+1$, the two diagonal pairings are $\beta(x_uT_i,x_u)=\beta(x_u,x_uT_i)=0$ and $\beta(x_vT_i,x_v)=\beta(x_v,x_vT_i)=(q-1)q^{\ell(v)}$. The two off-diagonal pairings both equal $q^{\ell(v)}=q\,q^{\ell(u)}$ by the action in step 1.2. A singleton orbit contributes $q\,q^{\ell(d)}$ on its diagonal, and pairings between distinct orbit spans vanish. Thus $\beta(xT_i,y)=\beta(x,yT_i)$ on basis vectors and hence, by bilinearity, on all of $M(\lambda)$.

**Words, all of $H$, and restriction.** For every word $h=T_{i_1}\cdots T_{i_r}$ of generators and all $x,y\in M(\lambda)$ one has $\beta(xh,y)=\beta(x,yh^*)$, where $h^*=T_{i_r}\cdots T_{i_1}$: this follows from step 2.1 by induction on $r$, moving one generator at a time from the first to the second argument. Since the generators span $H$ as an $R$-algebra by [F3], every $h\in H$ is a finite $R$-linear combination of such words, and by [F2] the element $h^*$ is obtained from the same expression by reversing each word; bilinearity therefore gives $\beta(xh,y)=\beta(x,yh^*)$ for all $h\in H$. Finally $P(\lambda)$ is a right ideal contained in $M(\lambda)$ by [F1], so the same identity holds for $x,y\in P(\lambda)$; its restriction to $P(\lambda)$ is the DJ form of the statement.

**Base change.** Under a ring map $R\to R'$ with $q\mapsto q'\in(R')^\times$, the distinguished basis identifies $R'\otimes_RM(\lambda)$ with $M_{R'}(\lambda)$ and the diagonal weights specialize, identifying the scalar extension of $\beta$ with $\beta'$. The natural map $j:R'\otimes_RP(\lambda)\to M_{R'}(\lambda)$ has image $P_{R'}(\lambda)$: the vectors $z_\lambda T_w$ span $P(\lambda)$ and their images $z'_\lambda T'_w$ span $P_{R'}(\lambda)$. For pure tensors, and then by bilinearity, $\beta'(j(a\otimes p),j(b\otimes r))=ab\,\beta(p,r)$. This proves compatibility of the restricted forms along the natural map, without inferring injectivity of a tensor map from right exactness; the later split polytabloid basis establishes that this map is also an isomorphism. Contravariance specializes by the same identity.

The permutation form is well defined, symmetric and bilinear by step 1.1, is $H$-contravariant by step 3.1, and its restriction to $P(\lambda)$ satisfies the same identity; both forms are base-change compatible by step 4.1. Only the distinguished basis, inversion counts and the algebra structure of $H$ are used; no choice principle is used.

risk_review.notes: Checked the singleton and two-element generator orbits, all four pairings and extension to reversed words. Decreasing diagonal equals (q-1)q^ell(v); the row weights are units. The restriction is contravariant because zH is stable. Base change is a pullback identity along the surjective natural map, without a tensor-injectivity inference; no later splitting is used as a premise. Empty shape and zero ring are admitted.

Step 4.1 records that no choice principle is used; theta is defined on generators in step 1.1, the eigenspace classification iterates length-decreasing generators of the finite parabolic subgroup in step 2.2, and the dual basis of [F4] is unique.

citations.quote:
Let $n\ge0$ be an integer, with $S_0=\{1\}$ as in
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]. Let $A:=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ be the ring of Laurent polynomials in one
indeterminate $v$ over $\mathbb Z$. For $n\ge2$ the **generic type-A Hecke
algebra** $H_v(n)$ is the associative unital $A$-algebra presented by generators
$T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$ and the relations
$$T_i^2=(v-1)T_i+v\quad(1\le i<n),\qquad T_iT_{i+1}T_i=T_{i+1}T_iT_{i+1}\quad(1\le i\le n-2),\qquad T_iT_j=T_jT_i\quad(1\le i,j<n,\ |i-j|>1),$$
that is, the quotient of the free unital associative $A$-algebra on
$T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$ by the two-sided ideal generated by these relators. The
first relation is written in the **RG-13 quadratic normalization**
$(T_i-v)(T_i+1)=0$, equivalent to the displayed form over $A$. For $n\le1$ there
are no generators and we set $H_v(n):=A$.

**Standard basis elements.** Let $S_n=\operatorname{Sym}(\{1,\dots,n\})$ with
simple transpositions $s_i=(i\ i+1)$
([[def-symmetric-group]]), and let $w\in S_n$ have inversion length $\ell(w)=\ell$
([[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]). Choose a reduced expression
$w=s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_\ell}$, that is, a word of the minimal length $\ell(w)$
representing $w$, and put
$$T_w:=T_{i_1}\cdots T_{i_\ell}\in H_v(n),$$
the empty product when $w$ is the identity of $S_n$, so that $T_w=1$ for that
element. That $T_w$ is independent of the chosen reduced expression, and that
the elements $T_w$ form an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$, is proved in the
standard-basis theorem below
([[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]); the notation
distinguishes the generator $T_i$ with $1\le i\le n-1$ from $T_w$ for the group
element $w$.

**Specializations.** Let $R$ be a commutative $A$-algebra with structure map
$\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]\to R$, $v\mapsto v_0$, and suppose $v_0\in R^\times$. The
**specialization** of $H_v(n)$ at $v_0$ is the $R$-algebra
$R\otimes_AH_v(n)$; it is presented over $R$ by the images of $T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$
subject to the same relations with $v$ replaced by $v_0$, and we write $H_{v_0}(n)$
for it. Two specializations are used on this page: $v\mapsto1$, where the
quadratic relation becomes $T_i^2=1$ together with the braid and commutation
relations, and $v\mapsto q$, where $q$ is the prime power defining
$\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb F_q)$; the latter specializes the generic algebra to
the Hecke algebra attached to the finite general linear group. The condition
$v_0\in R^\times$ is part of the definition of a specialization and, for a nonzero coefficient ring $R$, excludes $v_0=0$. The zero ring
is allowed: its unique element is a unit and its specialization is the zero algebra.

In the generic type-A Hecke algebra $H_v(n)$ over $A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ with
generators $T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$, the quadratic relations
$(T_i-v)(T_i+1)=0$, the braid relations and the distant commutations, and with
$T_w$ the product of the $T_i$ along a reduced word for $w\in S_n$
([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]):

1. $\{T_w:w\in S_n\}$ is an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$; in particular $H_v(n)$ is
free of rank $n!$ over $A$;
2. for every $w\in S_n$ and every $1\le i\le n-1$,
$$T_wT_i=T_{ws_i}\quad\text{if }\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)+1,\qquad T_wT_i=(v-1)T_w+v\,T_{ws_i}\quad\text{if }\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)-1,$$
where $\ell$ is the inversion length of $S_n$
([[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]); consequently the rule rewrites
every monomial in the generators as an $A$-linear combination of the $T_w$.

No choice principle is used.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $q\in R^\times$, let $n\ge0$, and let
$H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$ be the type-A Hecke algebra over $R$ with generators
$T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$, quadratic relations $(T_i-q)(T_i+1)=0$, braid and distant
commutation relations, and standard basis $\{T_w:w\in S_n\}$
([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]],
[[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]); here
$\ell(w)$ is the inversion length of $w\in S_n$
([[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]). All modules below are right
modules.

**The star anti-involution.** Let $\sigma\mapsto\sigma^*$ be the unique
$R$-algebra anti-automorphism of $H$ with $T_i^*=T_i$ for every generator: it
exists because reversal of words preserves the ideal of defining relations
(the quadratic and braid relators are fixed, while a distant commutation relator is sent to its negative), so reversal descends from the free algebra to $H$, and it is
unique because the generators generate $H$. On the standard basis
$T_w^*=T_{w^{-1}}$, since reversing a reduced word for $w$ is a reduced word
for $w^{-1}$.

**Tableau conventions.** Write $t\cdot\sigma$ for the right action of $S_n$ on
tableaux defined by $(t\cdot\sigma)(c):=\sigma^{-1}(t(c))$; it is the inverse
of the left action $(\sigma\cdot t)(c)=\sigma(t(c))$ of
[[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]], and it is a right action.
A $\lambda$-tableau is **row standard** when its entries strictly increase
along every row; columns are not constrained. Let $t^\lambda$ be the row-filled
$\lambda$-tableau, whose row $i$ carries
$\lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_{i-1}+1,\dots,\lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_i$ from left
to right, and let $t_\lambda$ be the column-filled $\lambda$-tableau, whose
column $j$ carries consecutive integers downward; equivalently
$t_\lambda(i,j)=t^{\lambda'}(j,i)$, so that $t_\lambda$ is the transpose of
$t^{\lambda'}$ ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]).

**The row subgroup and the coset representatives.** Let $S_\lambda$ be the
**row subgroup** of $\lambda$, the subgroup of $S_n$ preserving every row of
$t^\lambda$; writing
$$B_i:=\{\lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_{i-1}+1,\ \lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_{i-1}+2,\ \dots,\ \lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_i\}$$
for the $i$-th row block of $t^\lambda$, one has
$S_\lambda=S(B_1)\times\cdots\times S(B_k)$, the direct product of the
symmetric groups of the individual row blocks. Let
$$D_\lambda:=\{d\in S_n:t^\lambda\cdot d\text{ is row standard}\}.$$
This is the set of minimal-length right coset representatives of $S_\lambda$ in
$S_n$: every right coset $S_\lambda d$ has exactly one element $d_0$ for which
$t^\lambda\cdot d_0$ is row standard, and it satisfies
$\ell(wd_0)=\ell(w)+\ell(d_0)$ for all $w\in S_\lambda$
([[lem-dj-bridge-row-permutation-module-standard-action]]). Let
$w_\lambda\in S_n$ be the unique element with $t^\lambda\cdot w_\lambda=t_\lambda$;
existence and uniqueness hold because the action of $S_n$ on $\lambda$-tableaux
is free and transitive.

**Generators and modules.** For a partition $\lambda\vdash n$ put
$$x_\lambda:=\sum_{w\in S_\lambda}T_w,\qquad y_\lambda:=\sum_{w\in S_\lambda}(-q)^{-\ell(w)}T_w,\qquad z_\lambda:=x_\lambda T_{w_\lambda}y_{\lambda'},$$
where $\lambda'$ is the conjugate partition of $\lambda$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). The **row
permutation module** is the right ideal $M(\lambda):=x_\lambda H\subseteq H$,
and the **ordinary Dipper-James polytabloid module** is
$P(\lambda):=z_\lambda H\subseteq M(\lambda)$; $z_\lambda$ is its polytabloid
generator.

**The forms.** The **permutation form** is the $R$-bilinear form $\beta$ on
$M(\lambda)$ determined on the distinguished family
$\{x_\lambda T_d:d\in D_\lambda\}$ by
$$\beta(x_\lambda T_d,x_\lambda T_e)=\delta_{d,e}q^{\ell(d)}\qquad(d,e\in D_\lambda),$$
and the **DJ form** is the restriction of $\beta$ to $P(\lambda)$. That family
is an $R$-basis of $M(\lambda)$
([[lem-dj-bridge-row-permutation-module-standard-action]]), so the displayed
values define a unique bilinear form; the family is $\{x_\varnothing\}=\{1\}$
for the empty partition.

**Small cases and base change.** For $\lambda=\varnothing$ set
$x_\varnothing=y_\varnothing=z_\varnothing=1$, so that
$M(\varnothing)=P(\varnothing)=R$ and $\beta$ is the standard form; for
$n=0,1$ there are no generators and $H=R$. Every base change
$A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]\to R$, $v\mapsto q$, with $q\in R^\times$, produces all
objects above over $R$ by the same formulas; the suppliers of this page prove
that the distinguished families and the form are compatible with such base
change. No choice principle is used.

In the notation of
[[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]], for every
commutative ring $R$ and every $q\in R^\times$:

1. $M(\lambda)$ is free with basis $\{x_\lambda T_d:d\in D_\lambda\}$;

2. $x_\lambda T_w=q^{\ell(w)}x_\lambda$ and $T_wx_\lambda=q^{\ell(w)}x_\lambda$
for every $w\in S_\lambda$, and $x_\lambda^*=x_\lambda$;

3. if $d\in D_\lambda$, $t=t^\lambda\cdot d$ and $s=t\cdot s_i=t^\lambda\cdot d'$, then
$$x_\lambda T_dT_i=\begin{cases}q\,x_\lambda T_d,&s\text{ is not row standard},\\ x_\lambda T_{d'},&s\text{ is row standard and }\ell(d')>\ell(d),\\ q\,x_\lambda T_{d'}+(q-1)x_\lambda T_d,&s\text{ is row standard and }\ell(d')<\ell(d);\end{cases}$$

4. the basis and the action formulas are compatible with every base change
$R\to R'$ along a ring map sending $q$ to a unit.

No choice principle is used.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $n\in\mathbb N$, let $R^n$ be the free
$R$-module on an $n$-element set with standard basis $e_1,\ldots,e_n$
([[def-free-module-on-a-set-and-standard-basis]]), and let $N$ be an
$R$-module. Write $N^n$ for the direct sum of $n$ copies of $N$
([[def-direct-sum-of-a-family-of-modules]]), which for a finite index set is the
coordinatewise product. Then

$$\Phi\colon\operatorname{Hom}_R(R^n,N)\longrightarrow N^n,\qquad \Phi(f)=\big(f(e_1),\ldots,f(e_n)\big),$$

is an isomorphism of $R$-modules, the source carrying the module structure of
[[lem-hom-module-over-a-commutative-ring]].

At $n=0$ both sides are the zero module.

Let $n\ge0$ be an integer, with $S_0=\{1\}$ as in
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]. Let $A:=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ be the ring of Laurent polynomials in one
indeterminate $v$ over $\mathbb Z$. For $n\ge2$ the **generic type-A Hecke
algebra** $H_v(n)$ is the associative unital $A$-algebra presented by generators
$T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$ and the relations
$$T_i^2=(v-1)T_i+v\quad(1\le i<n),\qquad T_iT_{i+1}T_i=T_{i+1}T_iT_{i+1}\quad(1\le i\le n-2),\qquad T_iT_j=T_jT_i\quad(1\le i,j<n,\ |i-j|>1),$$
that is, the quotient of the free unital associative $A$-algebra on
$T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$ by the two-sided ideal generated by these relators. The
first relation is written in the **RG-13 quadratic normalization**
$(T_i-v)(T_i+1)=0$, equivalent to the displayed form over $A$. For $n\le1$ there
are no generators and we set $H_v(n):=A$.

**Standard basis elements.** Let $S_n=\operatorname{Sym}(\{1,\dots,n\})$ with
simple transpositions $s_i=(i\ i+1)$
([[def-symmetric-group]]), and let $w\in S_n$ have inversion length $\ell(w)=\ell$
([[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]). Choose a reduced expression
$w=s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_\ell}$, that is, a word of the minimal length $\ell(w)$
representing $w$, and put
$$T_w:=T_{i_1}\cdots T_{i_\ell}\in H_v(n),$$
the empty product when $w$ is the identity of $S_n$, so that $T_w=1$ for that
element. That $T_w$ is independent of the chosen reduced expression, and that
the elements $T_w$ form an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$, is proved in the
standard-basis theorem below
([[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]); the notation
distinguishes the generator $T_i$ with $1\le i\le n-1$ from $T_w$ for the group
element $w$.

**Specializations.** Let $R$ be a commutative $A$-algebra with structure map
$\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]\to R$, $v\mapsto v_0$, and suppose $v_0\in R^\times$. The
**specialization** of $H_v(n)$ at $v_0$ is the $R$-algebra
$R\otimes_AH_v(n)$; it is presented over $R$ by the images of $T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$
subject to the same relations with $v$ replaced by $v_0$, and we write $H_{v_0}(n)$
for it. Two specializations are used on this page: $v\mapsto1$, where the
quadratic relation becomes $T_i^2=1$ together with the braid and commutation
relations, and $v\mapsto q$, where $q$ is the prime power defining
$\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb F_q)$; the latter specializes the generic algebra to
the Hecke algebra attached to the finite general linear group. The condition
$v_0\in R^\times$ is part of the definition of a specialization and, for a nonzero coefficient ring $R$, excludes $v_0=0$. The zero ring
is allowed: its unique element is a unit and its specialization is the zero algebra.

derivations.claim: **The automorphism and its first properties.** Put $\theta(T_i):=(q-1)-T_i$. Since $T_i^{-1}=q^{-1}(T_i-(q-1))$ by [F1], one has $\theta(T_i)=-qT_i^{-1}$. The assignment satisfies the Hecke relations: $\theta(T_i)^2=(q-1)^2-2(q-1)T_i+T_i^2=(q-1)^2-2(q-1)T_i+(q-1)T_i+q=(q-1)\theta(T_i)+q$; the braid relation holds because $\theta(T_i)=-qT_i^{-1}$ multiplies every generator by the same scalar $-q$, and inverses satisfy the braid relations; the distant commutation holds similarly, and the scalar squares cancel. Since $H$ is presented by these relations, the assignment extends uniquely to an $R$-algebra endomorphism $\theta$ of $H$; applying it twice fixes each generator, so $\theta^2=\mathrm{id}_H$ by [F2] and $\theta$ is an involutive automorphism. For a reduced word $w=s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_\ell}$ one gets $\theta(T_w)=(-q)^\ell T_{i_1}^{-1}\cdots T_{i_\ell}^{-1}=(-q)^{\ell(w)}T_{w^{-1}}^{-1}$, and $\theta$ commutes with $*$ because both sides of $\theta(T_w^*)=(-q)^{\ell(w)}T_w^{-1}$ and $\theta(T_w)^*=(-q)^{\ell(w)}T_{w^{-1}}^{-*}=(-q)^{\ell(w)}T_w^{-1}$ agree. All generator images have coefficients in $\mathbb Z[q^{\pm1}]$, so $\theta$ is compatible with base change by [F5].

**Pullback of modules.** If $M$ is a right $H$-module, then $M^\theta$ with $m\cdot h:=m\theta(h)$ is a right $H$-module, because $(m\cdot h)\cdot k=m\theta(h)\theta(k)=m\theta(hk)=m\cdot(hk)$. Since $\theta$ is an involutive automorphism, the assignments $M\mapsto M^\theta$ on modules and $N\mapsto N$ on underlying $R$-modules are inverse bijections on submodules: a subset $N\subseteq M$ is closed under the old action if and only if it is closed under the new one, since $\theta$ is bijective and $\theta(H)=H$. Hence $(-)^\theta$ is exact, preserves submodules and quotients, and $(M^\theta)^\theta=M$; it also carries simple modules to simple modules and preserves the length of finite composition series with multiplicities, because the two module structures have exactly the same submodule lattice.

**Contragredient modules.** For a right $H$-module $M$, put $M^\circ:=\operatorname{Hom}_R(M,R)$ with $(f\cdot h)(m):=f(mh^*)$. Then $((f\cdot h)\cdot k)(m)=f(mk^*h^*)=f(m(hk)^*)$ by [F2], so $f\cdot(hk)=(f\cdot h)\cdot k$ and $M^\circ$ is a right $H$-module. If $M\cong R^r$ is finite free, then $M^\circ\cong R^r$ by [F4] applied with $N=R$, and the dual-basis identification is natural in $R$, so $(-)^\circ$ commutes with base change. Finally $(M^\theta)^\circ=(M^\circ)^\theta$: both have underlying module $\operatorname{Hom}_R(M,R)$, and for the two actions one computes $(f\cdot h)(m)=f(m\theta(h^*))$ for the first and $(f\cdot h)(m)=f(m\theta(h)^*)=f(m\theta(h^*))$ for the second, using that $\theta$ commutes with $*$ by step 1.1.

**The common eigenspace.** Let $H_\lambda$ be the $R$-span of $\{T_w:w\in S_\lambda\}$, the subalgebra generated by the $T_i$ with $s_i\in S_\lambda$; it is $\theta$-stable because $\theta(T_i)=(q-1)-T_i\in H_\lambda$. The element $\theta(x_\lambda)$ lies in $H_\lambda$ and satisfies $T_i\theta(x_\lambda)=\theta(\theta(T_i)x_\lambda)=\theta(((q-1)-T_i)x_\lambda)=\theta((q-1)x_\lambda-qx_\lambda)=-\theta(x_\lambda)$ for every generator $T_i$ of $S_\lambda$, by [F3]; so it is a common left eigenvector for eigenvalue $-1$. Conversely let $a=\sum_{w\in S_\lambda}a_wT_w\in H_\lambda$ satisfy $T_ia=-a$ for all these generators. Comparing in the expansion $T_ia=\sum_wa_wT_iT_w$, using the left multiplication rule of [F1], the coefficient of $T_v$ equals $qa_{s_iv}$ when $\ell(s_iv)=\ell(v)+1$ and equals $(q-1)a_v+a_{s_iv}$ when $\ell(s_iv)=\ell(v)-1$, and it must equal $-a_v$; the first case gives $a_{s_iv}=-q^{-1}a_v$, and the second gives the same relation with the roles of $v$ and $s_iv$ exchanged. Hence $a_{s_iu}=-q^{-1}a_u$ whenever $\ell(s_iu)=\ell(u)+1$. Every nonidentity $w\in S_\lambda$ is a length-increasing product of generators of $S_\lambda$: the permutation $w^{-1}$ restricted to some row block $B_r$ is not the identity, hence has an adjacent descent, which exhibits a generator $s_i$ of $S_\lambda$ with $\ell(s_iw)=\ell(w)-1$. Iterating, $a_w=(-q)^{-\ell(w)}a_1$ for all $w\in S_\lambda$, so $a=a_1y_\lambda$: the common eigenspace is exactly the free line $Ry_\lambda$, and it contains $\theta(x_\lambda)$.

**The case $q=1$.** At $q=1$ the quadratic relation is $T_i^2=1$, so $T_{w^{-1}}^{-1}=T_w$ and step 1.1 gives $\theta(T_w)=(-1)^{\ell(w)}T_w=\operatorname{sgn}(w)T_w$. The relations $T_i^2=1$, braid and distant commutation are the Coxeter relations of the adjacent transpositions of $S_n$, so the specialization $H_{R,1}(S_n)$ is the group algebra $R[S_n]$ with $T_w$ the group basis element $w$; the displayed identity then says that $\theta$ is the pullback along the sign automorphism $w\mapsto\operatorname{sgn}(w)w$. For $N=0$, as in the shapes $\varnothing$ and $(1^n)$, the unit below is $q^0=1$.

**The unit.** By step 2.2 write $\theta(x_\lambda)=c\,y_\lambda$ with $c\in R$. In the expansion $\theta(T_w)=\prod_j\theta(T_{i_j})=\prod_j((q-1)-T_{i_j})$ of a reduced word, every term other than the full product of the $-T_{i_j}$ has fewer than $\ell(w)$ generator factors and so cannot contribute to the standard basis element of length $N$; hence the coefficient of $T_{w_0(S_\lambda)}$ in $\theta(x_\lambda)=\sum_{w\in S_\lambda}\theta(T_w)$ is $(-1)^N$, the contribution of $w=w_0(S_\lambda)$ alone. In $c\,y_\lambda$ the coefficient of $T_{w_0(S_\lambda)}$ is $c(-q)^{-N}$, so $c=(-1)^N(-q)^N=q^N$. Therefore $\theta(x_\lambda)=q^Ny_\lambda$, and applying the involution $\theta$ and using $\theta(q^N)=q^N$ gives $\theta(y_\lambda)=q^{-N}x_\lambda$.

Statements (1), (2), (3) and (4) are established by steps 1.1, 1.2, 2.1 and 3.1, with the $q=1$ clause in step 2.3 and the unit $q^{\ell(w_0(S_\lambda))}$ displayed in step 3.1. Only the presentation of $H$, inversion counts, the standard basis and finite free duality are used; no choice principle is used.

citations.quote:
In the generic type-A Hecke algebra $H_v(n)$ over $A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ with
generators $T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$, the quadratic relations
$(T_i-v)(T_i+1)=0$, the braid relations and the distant commutations, and with
$T_w$ the product of the $T_i$ along a reduced word for $w\in S_n$
([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]):

1. $\{T_w:w\in S_n\}$ is an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$; in particular $H_v(n)$ is
free of rank $n!$ over $A$;
2. for every $w\in S_n$ and every $1\le i\le n-1$,
$$T_wT_i=T_{ws_i}\quad\text{if }\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)+1,\qquad T_wT_i=(v-1)T_w+v\,T_{ws_i}\quad\text{if }\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)-1,$$
where $\ell$ is the inversion length of $S_n$
([[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]); consequently the rule rewrites
every monomial in the generators as an $A$-linear combination of the $T_w$.

No choice principle is used.

Let $n\ge0$ be an integer, with $S_0=\{1\}$ as in
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]. Let $A:=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ be the ring of Laurent polynomials in one
indeterminate $v$ over $\mathbb Z$. For $n\ge2$ the **generic type-A Hecke
algebra** $H_v(n)$ is the associative unital $A$-algebra presented by generators
$T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$ and the relations
$$T_i^2=(v-1)T_i+v\quad(1\le i<n),\qquad T_iT_{i+1}T_i=T_{i+1}T_iT_{i+1}\quad(1\le i\le n-2),\qquad T_iT_j=T_jT_i\quad(1\le i,j<n,\ |i-j|>1),$$
that is, the quotient of the free unital associative $A$-algebra on
$T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$ by the two-sided ideal generated by these relators. The
first relation is written in the **RG-13 quadratic normalization**
$(T_i-v)(T_i+1)=0$, equivalent to the displayed form over $A$. For $n\le1$ there
are no generators and we set $H_v(n):=A$.

**Standard basis elements.** Let $S_n=\operatorname{Sym}(\{1,\dots,n\})$ with
simple transpositions $s_i=(i\ i+1)$
([[def-symmetric-group]]), and let $w\in S_n$ have inversion length $\ell(w)=\ell$
([[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]). Choose a reduced expression
$w=s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_\ell}$, that is, a word of the minimal length $\ell(w)$
representing $w$, and put
$$T_w:=T_{i_1}\cdots T_{i_\ell}\in H_v(n),$$
the empty product when $w$ is the identity of $S_n$, so that $T_w=1$ for that
element. That $T_w$ is independent of the chosen reduced expression, and that
the elements $T_w$ form an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$, is proved in the
standard-basis theorem below
([[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]); the notation
distinguishes the generator $T_i$ with $1\le i\le n-1$ from $T_w$ for the group
element $w$.

**Specializations.** Let $R$ be a commutative $A$-algebra with structure map
$\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]\to R$, $v\mapsto v_0$, and suppose $v_0\in R^\times$. The
**specialization** of $H_v(n)$ at $v_0$ is the $R$-algebra
$R\otimes_AH_v(n)$; it is presented over $R$ by the images of $T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$
subject to the same relations with $v$ replaced by $v_0$, and we write $H_{v_0}(n)$
for it. Two specializations are used on this page: $v\mapsto1$, where the
quadratic relation becomes $T_i^2=1$ together with the braid and commutation
relations, and $v\mapsto q$, where $q$ is the prime power defining
$\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb F_q)$; the latter specializes the generic algebra to
the Hecke algebra attached to the finite general linear group. The condition
$v_0\in R^\times$ is part of the definition of a specialization and, for a nonzero coefficient ring $R$, excludes $v_0=0$. The zero ring
is allowed: its unique element is a unit and its specialization is the zero algebra.

In the notation of
[[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]], for every
commutative ring $R$ and every $q\in R^\times$:

1. $M(\lambda)$ is free with basis $\{x_\lambda T_d:d\in D_\lambda\}$;

2. $x_\lambda T_w=q^{\ell(w)}x_\lambda$ and $T_wx_\lambda=q^{\ell(w)}x_\lambda$
for every $w\in S_\lambda$, and $x_\lambda^*=x_\lambda$;

3. if $d\in D_\lambda$, $t=t^\lambda\cdot d$ and $s=t\cdot s_i=t^\lambda\cdot d'$, then
$$x_\lambda T_dT_i=\begin{cases}q\,x_\lambda T_d,&s\text{ is not row standard},\\ x_\lambda T_{d'},&s\text{ is row standard and }\ell(d')>\ell(d),\\ q\,x_\lambda T_{d'}+(q-1)x_\lambda T_d,&s\text{ is row standard and }\ell(d')<\ell(d);\end{cases}$$

4. the basis and the action formulas are compatible with every base change
$R\to R'$ along a ring map sending $q$ to a unit.

No choice principle is used.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $q\in R^\times$, let $n\ge0$, and let
$H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$ be the type-A Hecke algebra over $R$ with generators
$T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$, quadratic relations $(T_i-q)(T_i+1)=0$, braid and distant
commutation relations, and standard basis $\{T_w:w\in S_n\}$
([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]],
[[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]); here
$\ell(w)$ is the inversion length of $w\in S_n$
([[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]). All modules below are right
modules.

**The star anti-involution.** Let $\sigma\mapsto\sigma^*$ be the unique
$R$-algebra anti-automorphism of $H$ with $T_i^*=T_i$ for every generator: it
exists because reversal of words preserves the ideal of defining relations
(the quadratic and braid relators are fixed, while a distant commutation relator is sent to its negative), so reversal descends from the free algebra to $H$, and it is
unique because the generators generate $H$. On the standard basis
$T_w^*=T_{w^{-1}}$, since reversing a reduced word for $w$ is a reduced word
for $w^{-1}$.

**Tableau conventions.** Write $t\cdot\sigma$ for the right action of $S_n$ on
tableaux defined by $(t\cdot\sigma)(c):=\sigma^{-1}(t(c))$; it is the inverse
of the left action $(\sigma\cdot t)(c)=\sigma(t(c))$ of
[[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]], and it is a right action.
A $\lambda$-tableau is **row standard** when its entries strictly increase
along every row; columns are not constrained. Let $t^\lambda$ be the row-filled
$\lambda$-tableau, whose row $i$ carries
$\lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_{i-1}+1,\dots,\lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_i$ from left
to right, and let $t_\lambda$ be the column-filled $\lambda$-tableau, whose
column $j$ carries consecutive integers downward; equivalently
$t_\lambda(i,j)=t^{\lambda'}(j,i)$, so that $t_\lambda$ is the transpose of
$t^{\lambda'}$ ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]).

**The row subgroup and the coset representatives.** Let $S_\lambda$ be the
**row subgroup** of $\lambda$, the subgroup of $S_n$ preserving every row of
$t^\lambda$; writing
$$B_i:=\{\lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_{i-1}+1,\ \lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_{i-1}+2,\ \dots,\ \lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_i\}$$
for the $i$-th row block of $t^\lambda$, one has
$S_\lambda=S(B_1)\times\cdots\times S(B_k)$, the direct product of the
symmetric groups of the individual row blocks. Let
$$D_\lambda:=\{d\in S_n:t^\lambda\cdot d\text{ is row standard}\}.$$
This is the set of minimal-length right coset representatives of $S_\lambda$ in
$S_n$: every right coset $S_\lambda d$ has exactly one element $d_0$ for which
$t^\lambda\cdot d_0$ is row standard, and it satisfies
$\ell(wd_0)=\ell(w)+\ell(d_0)$ for all $w\in S_\lambda$
([[lem-dj-bridge-row-permutation-module-standard-action]]). Let
$w_\lambda\in S_n$ be the unique element with $t^\lambda\cdot w_\lambda=t_\lambda$;
existence and uniqueness hold because the action of $S_n$ on $\lambda$-tableaux
is free and transitive.

**Generators and modules.** For a partition $\lambda\vdash n$ put
$$x_\lambda:=\sum_{w\in S_\lambda}T_w,\qquad y_\lambda:=\sum_{w\in S_\lambda}(-q)^{-\ell(w)}T_w,\qquad z_\lambda:=x_\lambda T_{w_\lambda}y_{\lambda'},$$
where $\lambda'$ is the conjugate partition of $\lambda$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). The **row
permutation module** is the right ideal $M(\lambda):=x_\lambda H\subseteq H$,
and the **ordinary Dipper-James polytabloid module** is
$P(\lambda):=z_\lambda H\subseteq M(\lambda)$; $z_\lambda$ is its polytabloid
generator.

**The forms.** The **permutation form** is the $R$-bilinear form $\beta$ on
$M(\lambda)$ determined on the distinguished family
$\{x_\lambda T_d:d\in D_\lambda\}$ by
$$\beta(x_\lambda T_d,x_\lambda T_e)=\delta_{d,e}q^{\ell(d)}\qquad(d,e\in D_\lambda),$$
and the **DJ form** is the restriction of $\beta$ to $P(\lambda)$. That family
is an $R$-basis of $M(\lambda)$
([[lem-dj-bridge-row-permutation-module-standard-action]]), so the displayed
values define a unique bilinear form; the family is $\{x_\varnothing\}=\{1\}$
for the empty partition.

**Small cases and base change.** For $\lambda=\varnothing$ set
$x_\varnothing=y_\varnothing=z_\varnothing=1$, so that
$M(\varnothing)=P(\varnothing)=R$ and $\beta$ is the standard form; for
$n=0,1$ there are no generators and $H=R$. Every base change
$A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]\to R$, $v\mapsto q$, with $q\in R^\times$, produces all
objects above over $R$ by the same formulas; the suppliers of this page prove
that the distinguished families and the form are compatible with such base
change. No choice principle is used.

For every commutative ring $R$ and $q\in R^\times$:

1. $\theta(T_i):=(q-1)-T_i=-qT_i^{-1}$ extends uniquely to an involutive
$R$-algebra automorphism $\theta$ of $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$, with
$\theta(T_w)=(-q)^{\ell(w)}T_{w^{-1}}^{-1}$; $\theta$ commutes with the star
anti-involution $*$ and is compatible with every base change.

2. For a right $H$-module $M$, the pullback $M^\theta$ (same underlying
$R$-module, action $m\cdot h:=m\theta(h)$) is a right $H$-module; $(-)^\theta$
is exact, preserves submodules, quotients, finite composition multiplicities and
simplicity, and $(M^\theta)^\theta=M$.

3. The star-contragredient $M^\circ:=\operatorname{Hom}_R(M,R)$ with
$(f\cdot h)(m):=f(mh^*)$ is a right $H$-module; for finite free $M$ it is finite
free of the same rank, $(-)^\circ$ commutes with base change, and
$(M^\theta)^\circ=(M^\circ)^\theta$.

4. For every partition $\lambda\vdash n$, if $w_0(S_\lambda)$ is the longest
element of the row subgroup, then
$$\theta(x_\lambda)=q^{\ell(w_0(S_\lambda))}y_\lambda,\qquad \theta(y_\lambda)=q^{-\ell(w_0(S_\lambda))}x_\lambda.$$
In particular $\theta(x_\lambda)$ and $y_\lambda$ differ by the unit
$q^{\ell(w_0(S_\lambda))}$, and this unit factor must be carried through every
form comparison. At $q=1$, $\theta$ is the pullback along the sign automorphism
$w\mapsto\operatorname{sgn}(w)w$ of $R[S_n]$.

No choice principle is used.

Let $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ be partitions of the same integer $n$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). We say that
$\lambda$ **dominates** $\mu$, and write $\lambda\unrhd\mu$, exactly when
$$\sum_{i=1}^{r}\lambda_i\;\ge\;\sum_{i=1}^{r}\mu_i\qquad\text{for every }r\ge1,$$
where each sequence is padded with zeros beyond its number of parts; since both
partitions have total $n$, both sides equal $n$ for all $r$ at least the number
of parts of either, so the condition is a finite family of inequalities between
integers. We write $\lambda\rhd\mu$ when $\lambda\unrhd\mu$ and
$\lambda\ne\mu$. The relation $\unrhd$ is the **dominance order** on the
partitions of $n$; we call $\lambda$ and $\mu$ **incomparable** when neither
$\lambda\unrhd\mu$ nor $\mu\unrhd\lambda$ holds.

Because it is defined by a family of non-strict inequalities between integers,
$\unrhd$ is reflexive and transitive. It is also antisymmetric: if
$\lambda\unrhd\mu$ and $\mu\unrhd\lambda$, then the prefix sums of $\lambda$ and
of $\mu$ are equal for every $r\ge1$, and subtracting consecutive prefix sums
gives $\lambda_i=\mu_i$ for every $i$ (both sequences are eventually zero).
Hence $\unrhd$ is a partial order on the set of partitions of $n$. For $n\ge1$,
the partition $(n)$ is its unique maximum and the partition $(1^n)$ its unique
minimum: for every $\mu\vdash n$ and every $r\ge1$ one has
$$\min(r,n)=\sum_{i\le r}(1^n)_i\;\le\;\sum_{i\le r}\mu_i\;\le\;n=\sum_{i\le r}(n)_i .$$

For $n=0$ the order is the trivial order on the one-element set
$\{\varnothing\}$.

Suppose $\alpha$ is not dominated by $
u'$. By step 1.4 every double coset matrix has an entry at least $2$, so by step 4.1 every $x_\alpha T_dy_
u$ with $d\in S_n$ vanishes; since the $T_d$ are an $R$-basis of $H$ by [F1], $x_\alpha Hy_
u=0$. All structure constants lie in $\mathbb Z[q^{\pm1}]$, no factor $q+1$ is inverted, and no choice principle is used; for $n=0,1$ the groups are trivial and the claim is immediate.
