   $f^{\lambda'}=f^\lambda$ and carries the transported form
   $G_{\lambda'}^\theta$. No choice principle is used.

Let $A$ be a finite-dimensional algebra over a field and let $J=J(A)$. Then
$J$ is nilpotent, and the quotient algebra $A/J$ is semisimple.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^\times$ and $\lambda\vdash n$, and let $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ with its basis $\{m_t\}$, $P(\lambda)=z_\lambda H$, the permutation form $\beta$ on $M(\lambda)$ and the DJ form on $P(\lambda)$ be as in [[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]], [[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]] and [[lem-dj-bridge-integral-murphy-and-polytabloid-straightening]]. Then:

1. Setting $B_\lambda(m_s,p):=\beta(x_\lambda T_{d_\lambda(s)},p)$ for $s\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)$ and $p\in P(\lambda)$ defines an explicit $R$-bilinear pairing $B_\lambda\colon C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)\times P(\lambda)\to R$ that is $H$-balanced, $B_\lambda(mh,p)=B_\lambda(m,ph^*)$, and whose adjoint $c\mapsto B_\lambda(c,-)$ is an isomorphism of right $H$-modules $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)\to P(\lambda)^\circ$ onto the star-contragredient module of [[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]]. No nondegeneracy of the DJ form $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$ is required.

2. Equivalently, the kernel of the quotient map $M(\lambda)\to C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ is the orthogonal complement $P(\lambda)^\perp=\{a\in M(\lambda):\beta(a,p)=0\text{ for all }p\in P(\lambda)\}$, namely $M(\lambda)\cap I^{\rhd\lambda}$; the pairing matrices in the bases $\{m_s\}$ and $\{e_t\}$ have entries $B_\lambda(m_s,e_t)=q^{\ell(d_\lambda(s))}a_{d_\lambda(s),t}$ with $e_t=\sum_d a_{d,t}b_d$, and determinant a unit of $A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$. Their inverses are finite tableau formulas given by the adjugate divided by this unit.

3. All statements are compatible with every base change $A\to R$, $v\mapsto q$; the construction uses no generic semisimplicity, no nondegeneracy of $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$ and no choice principle.

Let $n\ge0$ be an integer, with $S_0=\{1\}$ as in
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]. Let $A:=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ be the ring of Laurent polynomials in one
indeterminate $v$ over $\mathbb Z$. For $n\ge2$ the **generic type-A Hecke
algebra** $H_v(n)$ is the associative unital $A$-algebra presented by generators
$T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$ and the relations
$$T_i^2=(v-1)T_i+v\quad(1\le i<n),\qquad T_iT_{i+1}T_i=T_{i+1}T_iT_{i+1}\quad(1\le i\le n-2),\qquad T_iT_j=T_jT_i\quad(1\le i,j<n,\ |i-j|>1),$$
that is, the quotient of the free unital associative $A$-algebra on
$T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$ by the two-sided ideal generated by these relators. The
first relation is written in the **RG-13 quadratic normalization**
$(T_i-v)(T_i+1)=0$, equivalent to the displayed form over $A$. For $n\le1$ there
are no generators and we set $H_v(n):=A$.

**Standard basis elements.** Let $S_n=\operatorname{Sym}(\{1,\dots,n\})$ with
simple transpositions $s_i=(i\ i+1)$
([[def-symmetric-group]]), and let $w\in S_n$ have inversion length $\ell(w)=\ell$
([[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]). Choose a reduced expression
$w=s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_\ell}$, that is, a word of the minimal length $\ell(w)$
representing $w$, and put
$$T_w:=T_{i_1}\cdots T_{i_\ell}\in H_v(n),$$
the empty product when $w$ is the identity of $S_n$, so that $T_w=1$ for that
element. That $T_w$ is independent of the chosen reduced expression, and that
the elements $T_w$ form an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$, is proved in the
standard-basis theorem below
([[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]); the notation
distinguishes the generator $T_i$ with $1\le i\le n-1$ from $T_w$ for the group
element $w$.

**Specializations.** Let $R$ be a commutative $A$-algebra with structure map
$\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]\to R$, $v\mapsto v_0$, and suppose $v_0\in R^\times$. The
**specialization** of $H_v(n)$ at $v_0$ is the $R$-algebra
$R\otimes_AH_v(n)$; it is presented over $R$ by the images of $T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$
subject to the same relations with $v$ replaced by $v_0$, and we write $H_{v_0}(n)$
for it. Two specializations are used on this page: $v\mapsto1$, where the
quadratic relation becomes $T_i^2=1$ together with the braid and commutation
relations, and $v\mapsto q$, where $q$ is the prime power defining
$\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb F_q)$; the latter specializes the generic algebra to
the Hecke algebra attached to the finite general linear group. The condition
$v_0\in R^\times$ is part of the definition of a specialization and, for a nonzero coefficient ring $R$, excludes $v_0=0$. The zero ring
is allowed: its unique element is a unit and its specialization is the zero algebra.

For every commutative ring $R$ and $q\in R^\times$:

1. $\theta(T_i):=(q-1)-T_i=-qT_i^{-1}$ extends uniquely to an involutive
$R$-algebra automorphism $\theta$ of $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$, with
$\theta(T_w)=(-q)^{\ell(w)}T_{w^{-1}}^{-1}$; $\theta$ commutes with the star
anti-involution $*$ and is compatible with every base change.

2. For a right $H$-module $M$, the pullback $M^\theta$ (same underlying
$R$-module, action $m\cdot h:=m\theta(h)$) is a right $H$-module; $(-)^\theta$
is exact, preserves submodules, quotients, finite composition multiplicities and
simplicity, and $(M^\theta)^\theta=M$.

3. The star-contragredient $M^\circ:=\operatorname{Hom}_R(M,R)$ with
$(f\cdot h)(m):=f(mh^*)$ is a right $H$-module; for finite free $M$ it is finite
free of the same rank, $(-)^\circ$ commutes with base change, and
$(M^\theta)^\circ=(M^\circ)^\theta$.

4. For every partition $\lambda\vdash n$, if $w_0(S_\lambda)$ is the longest
element of the row subgroup, then
$$\theta(x_\lambda)=q^{\ell(w_0(S_\lambda))}y_\lambda,\qquad \theta(y_\lambda)=q^{-\ell(w_0(S_\lambda))}x_\lambda.$$
In particular $\theta(x_\lambda)$ and $y_\lambda$ differ by the unit
$q^{\ell(w_0(S_\lambda))}$, and this unit factor must be carried through every
form comparison. At $q=1$, $\theta$ is the pullback along the sign automorphism
$w\mapsto\operatorname{sgn}(w)w$ of $R[S_n]$.

No choice principle is used.

derivations.claim: **The integral map.** Identify $C_{\mathrm M}(\mu)^\theta$ with $\theta(M(\mu))/\theta(K_\mu)$, where $K_\mu=M(\mu)\cap I^{\rhd\mu}$. By [F2], literal left multiplication by $q^{-N}x_\lambda T_{w_\lambda}$ kills $\theta(K_\mu)$ and induces the surjection $F:C_{\mathrm M}(\mu)^\theta\to P(\lambda)$ sending the class of $x_\mu$ to $z_\lambda$. In particular $F(m)=q^{-N}x_\lambda T_{w_\lambda}\theta(\widetilde m)$ for any row-module lift, independently of that lift. Both modules are free of rank $f^\mu=f^\lambda$; finite basis preimages give a right inverse of the square matrix of $F$, so its determinant is a unit and $F$ is an isomorphism. Set $\Phi_\lambda=F^{-1}$. Its $H$-linearity with the twisted target action gives $\Phi_\lambda(z_\lambda h)=m_0\theta(h)$, where this expression uses the ordinary action on the underlying Murphy module. All these matrices and their inverses lie in the universal Laurent ring and specialize by [F8].

**Generic uniqueness of the forms, after the integral isomorphism.** Work over $A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ with formal $q=v$ and $K=\mathbb Q(v)$. The matrix of the regular trace form $(a,b)\mapsto\operatorname{Tr}_K(L_{ab})$ has Laurent-polynomial entries. At $v=1$ its matrix is $n!$ times the permutation matrix $u\leftrightarrow u^{-1}$: in the regular group basis left multiplication by a nonidentity group element has trace zero, whereas the identity has trace $n!$. Its determinant is therefore nonzero, so the regular trace form is nonsingular over $K$. If $a\in J(H_K)$, every $ab$ is nilpotent by [F6], and $L_{ab}$ has trace zero; nondegeneracy forces $a=0$, so $H_K$ is semisimple. To justify the consequence used next, any quotient algebra of a finite-dimensional semisimple algebra has semisimple regular module: the images of its finitely many simple summands are simple or zero and span the quotient; selecting successively images not contained in their predecessors expresses it as a direct sum of simples. A square-zero two-sided ideal $J$ of such an algebra acts trivially on every simple module, since $JS$ is either $0$ or $S$ and the latter would force $J^2S=S$; it therefore annihilates the semisimple regular module and is zero. Each cellular layer is an ideal in a quotient of this semisimple algebra, with multiplication $(a\otimes b)(c\otimes d)=G_\mu(b,c)a\otimes d$. If $G_\mu$ had a nonzero radical, $(\operatorname{rad}G_\mu)\otimes C_{\mathrm M}(\mu)$ would be a nonzero square-zero ideal of that quotient, stable under its surrounding algebra by the cell law and contravariance, a contradiction. Thus $G_\mu$ is nonsingular, and the cellular rank-one operators realize the full matrix algebra on $C_{\mathrm M}(\mu)_K$. Every module endomorphism is scalar because it commutes with all matrix units; this conclusion also holds on the $\theta$-twist, since $\theta(H_K)=H_K$. On that twist, any contravariant form $B'$ defines an operator $U$ by $G_\mu^\theta(Ux,y)=B'(x,y)$. Contravariance and nonsingularity imply that $U$ commutes with the module action, so $B'$ is a scalar multiple of $G_\mu^\theta$. No generic argument was used to establish the integral map or basis.

**The exact generator computation.** The expansion in [F2] has distinct distinguished row-module vectors and length $L+\ell(u)$, so [F3] gives $$\beta(z_\lambda,z_\lambda)=\sum_{u\in S_\mu}q^{-2\ell(u)}q^{L+\ell(u)}=q^L\sum_{u\in S_\mu}q^{-\ell(u)}=q^{L-N}P_\mu(q).$$ The last equality pairs $u$ with $w_0(S_\mu)u$. The row identity $x_\mu T_u=q^{\ell(u)}x_\mu$ gives $x_\mu^2=P_\mu(q)x_\mu$, so the defining cell product in [F4] gives $G_\mu(m_0,m_0)=P_\mu(q)$. Therefore, with the specified normalization $\Phi_\lambda(z_\lambda)=m_0$, the only possible comparison unit is $u_\lambda(q)=q^{N-L}$. This computation uses the distinguished-basis definition of $\beta$, not any incorrectly unscaled trace identity.

**Universal form identity.** Transfer the DJ form to $C_{\mathrm M}(\mu)^\theta$ using $F=\Phi_\lambda^{-1}$: set $B'(c,d)=\beta(Fc,Fd)$. This is contravariant for the twisted action, as is $G_\mu^\theta$. Both are nonzero over $K$, since their respective generator values are $q^{L-N}P_\mu(q)$ and $P_\mu(q)$, nonzero in that field. Step 2.1 makes them proportional, and step 2.2 determines the scalar as $q^{N-L}$, proving $G_\mu^\theta(\Phi_\lambda x,\Phi_\lambda y)=q^{N-L}\beta(x,y)$ over $K$. Both sides have matrices in $A$; the injection $A\to K$ proves their equality already in $A$, and then [F8] specializes it to every commutative $R$ with unit parameter. No cancellation of $P_\mu(q)$ takes place after specialization.

**Radicals, divisibility, quotients and duality.** The unit form identity and the isomorphism $\Phi_\lambda$ identify the form radicals and yield $D^{\lambda}_{\mathrm{DJ}}\cong(D^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta$, including zero quotients. Over a field, a vector outside a nonzero cell-form radical generates its whole cell module: choose a vector pairing to $1$ and use its finite basis expansion in the cell rank-one action $x m_{uv}=G_\mu(x,m_u)m_v$. Thus every proper submodule lies in that radical, making it the unique maximal submodule and the nonzero form quotient the simple head; transfer this conclusion through $\Phi_\lambda$. If the form is identically zero only the zero form quotient is asserted, not a zero actual head. Over a PID with chosen prime $\pi$, the submodules $\{x:\beta(x,P(\lambda))\subseteq\pi^iR\}$ for every $i\ge0$ are identified with their Murphy counterparts because the forms differ by a unit; their reductions correspond as well. Applying step 1.1 to $\lambda'$ gives $P(\lambda')\cong C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)^\theta$. Compose with the same-shape perfect pairing [F7] and the commuting of star dual with $\theta$ in [F1] to obtain $P(\lambda')\cong P(\lambda)^{\circ,\theta}$. Empty shapes have $N=L=0$, $\Phi=1$ and unit $1$. This proves all clauses, using generic semisimplicity only for uniqueness of forms on an already integral module. No choice principle is used.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^\times$ and $\lambda\vdash n$, and write $\mu=\lambda'$, $L=\ell(w_\lambda)$ and $N=\ell(w_0(S_{\lambda'}))$. Let $P(\lambda)=z_\lambda H$ with its DJ form $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$, the cell module $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ with its Murphy form $G_{\lambda'}$, and the sign automorphism $\theta$ be as in [[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]], [[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]] and [[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]], and let $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')^\theta$ be the $\theta$-twisted cell module of [[lem-dj-bridge-theta-transport-of-the-cellular-structure]]. Then:

1. There is a base-change compatible isomorphism of right $H$-modules $$\Phi_\lambda\colon P(\lambda)\longrightarrow C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')^\theta,\qquad \Phi_\lambda(z_\lambda)=m_0,\quad \Phi_\lambda(z_\lambda h)=m_0\theta(h)\ \ (h\in H),$$ where $m_0$ is the class of $x_{\lambda'}$ in $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ and the right side is computed with the ordinary action on $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ and read in the twist; in particular $\Phi_\lambda(e_t)=m_0\theta(T_{d_{\lambda'}(t)})$ for $t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda')$. For a class $m\in C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ and any lift $\widetilde m\in M(\lambda')$, the inverse is $\Phi_\lambda^{-1}(m)=q^{-N}x_\lambda T_{w_\lambda}\theta(\widetilde m)$, independently of the chosen lift.

2. With $G_{\lambda'}^\theta$ the transported form of [[lem-dj-bridge-theta-transport-of-the-cellular-structure]] and $u_\lambda(q):=q^{\ell(w_0(S_{\lambda'}))-\ell(w_\lambda)}\in A^\times$, $$G_{\lambda'}^\theta(\Phi_\lambda x,\Phi_\lambda y)=u_\lambda(q)\,\beta_{P(\lambda)}(x,y)\qquad(x,y\in P(\lambda)),$$ over every commutative $R$ with $q\in R^\times$. No unnamed scalar and no potentially vanishing scalar occurs: $u_\lambda$ is the explicit unit $q^{N-L}$ in the fixed normalizations of this page.

3. Consequently $\Phi_\lambda$ maps the radical of $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$ onto the radical of $G_{\lambda'}^\theta$, the induced map between the quotients is an isomorphism, with the corresponding cell-form quotients $D^{\lambda}_{\mathrm{DJ}}\cong(D^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta$, including the zero-quotient case. Over a field, when the quotients are nonzero they are the simple heads; when the forms are identically zero, the displayed quotients are zero and no assertion about the actual module heads is made. Over a PID with a chosen prime, the unit-scaled form identity preserves all divisibility submodules and their reductions. One also obtains $P(\lambda')\cong P(\lambda)^{\circ,\theta}$ with the exact position of the dual and the twist, separating same-shape duality from conjugate-sign transport. No choice principle is used.

1. $\theta(T_i):=(q-1)-T_i=-qT_i^{-1}$ extends uniquely to an involutive
$R$-algebra automorphism $\theta$ of $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$, with
$\theta(T_w)=(-q)^{\ell(w)}T_{w^{-1}}^{-1}$; $\theta$ commutes with the star
anti-involution $*$ and is compatible with every base change.

2. For a right $H$-module $M$, the pullback $M^\theta$ (same underlying
$R$-module, action $m\cdot h:=m\theta(h)$) is a right $H$-module; $(-)^\theta$
is exact, preserves submodules, quotients, finite composition multiplicities and

3. The star-contragredient $M^\circ:=\operatorname{Hom}_R(M,R)$ with

4. For every partition $\lambda\vdash n$, if $w_0(S_\lambda)$ is the longest
element of the row subgroup, then
$$\theta(x_\lambda)=q^{\ell(w_0(S_\lambda))}y_\lambda,\qquad \theta(y_\lambda)=q^{-\ell(w_0(S_\lambda))}x_\lambda.$$
In particular $\theta(x_\lambda)$ and $y_\lambda$ differ by the unit

No choice principle is used.

Let $n\ge0$, let $\lambda\vdash n$, and let $\Omega_\lambda$ be the finite set
of $\lambda$-tabloids; for a $\lambda$-tableau $t$ write $\{t\}$ for its
tabloid ([[def-young-subgroup-tabloid-and-permutation-module]]). The
**integral tabloid module** is the free abelian group on $\Omega_\lambda$,

$$M^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}:=\mathbb Z^{(\Omega_\lambda)} =\Bigl\{\sum_{T\in\Omega_\lambda}a_T\,T:\ a_T\in\mathbb Z,\ \text{only finitely many }a_T\ne0\Bigr\},$$

with the tabloids as standard $\mathbb Z$-basis
([[def-free-module-on-a-set-and-standard-basis]]). The left action of $S_n$ on
tabloids extends $\mathbb Z$-linearly to $M^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}$, so that
$M^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}$ is a $\mathbb Z[S_n]$-module. For every $\lambda$-tableau
$t$ put

$$\kappa_t:=\sum_{\gamma\in C_t}\operatorname{sgn}(\gamma)\gamma \in\mathbb Z[S_n],\qquad e_t:=\kappa_t\cdot\{t\}=\sum_{\gamma\in C_t}\operatorname{sgn}(\gamma)\, \{\gamma\cdot t\}\in M^\lambda_{\mathbb Z},$$

the **integral column polytabloid**; every coefficient lies in
$\{0,1,-1\}$ ([[def-column-antisymmetrizer-polytabloid-and-specht-module]]).
The **integral Specht lattice** is the $\mathbb Z[S_n]$-submodule

$$S^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}:=\text{the }\mathbb Z\text{-span of } \{\,e_s:\ s\text{ a }\lambda\text{-tableau}\,\}\subseteq M^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}.$$

For a commutative ring $R$ let $M^\lambda_R:=R^{(\Omega_\lambda)}$ be the free
$R$-module on the tabloids and let $S^\lambda_R\subseteq M^\lambda_R$ be the
$R$-span of the polytabloids $\sum_{\gamma\in C_t}\operatorname{sgn}(\gamma)
\{\gamma\cdot t\}$, $t$ a $\lambda$-tableau. The **standard polytabloids** are
the $e_s$ with $s$ a standard $\lambda$-tableau
([[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]]).

This item records three facts. First, the standard polytabloids form a
$\mathbb Z$-basis of $S^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}$, so the integral Specht lattice has
explicit finite rank. Second, for every commutative ring $R$ the canonical map
$R\otimes_{\mathbb Z}S^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}\to R\otimes_{\mathbb Z}
M^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}\cong M^\lambda_R$ is injective onto $S^\lambda_R$: the
lattice is a direct summand of the free tabloid module and is compatible with
base change, including rings of prime characteristic. Third, for
$\lambda=\varnothing$ the module has rank one and is generated by the empty
polytabloid.

Let $F$ be a field, $n\ge0$, $\lambda\vdash n$, and let $\lambda'$ be the
conjugate partition. Write $\Omega_\lambda$ for the finite set of
$\lambda$-tabloids and let
$$M^\lambda_F=F^{(\Omega_\lambda)},\qquad S^\lambda_F\subseteq M^\lambda_F,\qquad \kappa_t=\sum_{\gamma\in C_t}\operatorname{sgn}(\gamma)\gamma,\qquad e_t=\kappa_t\{t\}$$
be the field-valued tabloid module, the span of the polytabloids inside it,
the column antisymmetrizer, and the polytabloid of a $\lambda$-tableau $t$
([[def-young-subgroup-tabloid-and-permutation-module]],
[[def-column-antisymmetrizer-polytabloid-and-specht-module]]). Let
$$\beta_F:M^\lambda_F\times M^\lambda_F\longrightarrow F$$
be the $F$-bilinear form for which the tabloid basis is orthonormal
([[def-integral-tabloid-bilinear-form-and-specht-gram-matrix]]), and for a
subspace $V\subseteq M^\lambda_F$ put
$$V^\perp:=\{x\in M^\lambda_F:\beta_F(x,v)=0\text{ for all }v\in V\}.$$

Let $\operatorname{sgn}$ be the sign representation of $S_n$ on the line
$F w$, so that $\sigma\cdot w=\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)w$
([[def-sign-representation-and-restriction-of-a-representation]]), and let
$$S^\lambda_F\otimes\operatorname{sgn}$$
be the tensor product of $F[S_n]$-modules with the diagonal action
$\sigma\cdot(x\otimes w):=(\sigma\cdot x)\otimes(\sigma\cdot w)$, a
finite-dimensional $F[S_n]$-module
([[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]). For a
finite-dimensional $F[S_n]$-module $D$ the **dual** is
$D^*=\operatorname{Hom}_F(D,F)$ with $(\sigma\cdot f)(v):=f(\sigma^{-1}v)$.

Fix the **row-filled** $\lambda$-tableau $t_0$, whose $i$-th row carries the
block $B_i=\{\lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_{i-1}+1,\dots,\lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_i\}$
in increasing order, and let $t_0^{\mathsf T}$ be its transpose, a
$\lambda'$-tableau. For a $\lambda'$-tableau $u$ let $\sigma_u\in S_n$ be the
unique permutation with $\sigma_u\cdot t_0^{\mathsf T}=u$, and let
$u^{\mathsf T}$ be the transpose of $u$, a $\lambda$-tableau. Define an
$F$-linear map on the tabloid basis of $M^{\lambda'}_F$ by
$$\theta(\{u\}):=\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma_u)\,\bigl(e_{u^{\mathsf T}}\otimes w\bigr) \ \in\ S^\lambda_F\otimes\operatorname{sgn}.$$

**Lemma.** With this notation:

1. $\theta$ does not depend on the chosen representative $u$ of the tabloid
   $\{u\}$; it is a well-defined $F[S_n]$-module homomorphism
   $\theta:M^{\lambda'}_F\to S^\lambda_F\otimes\operatorname{sgn}$ with
   $\theta(\{t_0^{\mathsf T}\})=e_{t_0}\otimes w$.
2. $\theta$ is surjective and
   $\ker\theta=(S^{\lambda'}_F)^\perp$.
3. Consequently $\theta$ induces $F[S_n]$-isomorphisms
   $$M^{\lambda'}_F/(S^{\lambda'}_F)^\perp\cong S^\lambda_F\otimes\operatorname{sgn}, \qquad\text{hence}\qquad S^\lambda_F\otimes\operatorname{sgn}\cong (S^{\lambda'}_F)^*,$$
   the second being the composite with $x\mapsto\beta_F(x,\cdot)|_{S^{\lambda'}_F}$.

No nondegeneracy of $\beta_F$ restricted to $S^{\lambda'}_F$ is assumed, and
the statement includes every prime characteristic, the case $n=0$, and the
case $F=\mathbb Q$ used in step 2.2. No step divides by a group order, none
uses positivity or averaging, and none uses characteristic zero beyond the
explicitly separated rational computation in steps 2.2 and 3.1.

Let $n\ge0$ be an integer, with $S_0=\{1\}$ as in
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]. Let $A:=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ be the ring of Laurent polynomials in one
indeterminate $v$ over $\mathbb Z$. For $n\ge2$ the **generic type-A Hecke
algebra** $H_v(n)$ is the associative unital $A$-algebra presented by generators
$T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$ and the relations
$$T_i^2=(v-1)T_i+v\quad(1\le i<n),\qquad T_iT_{i+1}T_i=T_{i+1}T_iT_{i+1}\quad(1\le i\le n-2),\qquad T_iT_j=T_jT_i\quad(1\le i,j<n,\ |i-j|>1),$$
that is, the quotient of the free unital associative $A$-algebra on
$T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$ by the two-sided ideal generated by these relators. The
first relation is written in the **RG-13 quadratic normalization**
$(T_i-v)(T_i+1)=0$, equivalent to the displayed form over $A$. For $n\le1$ there
are no generators and we set $H_v(n):=A$.

**Standard basis elements.** Let $S_n=\operatorname{Sym}(\{1,\dots,n\})$ with
simple transpositions $s_i=(i\ i+1)$
([[def-symmetric-group]]), and let $w\in S_n$ have inversion length $\ell(w)=\ell$
([[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]). Choose a reduced expression
$w=s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_\ell}$, that is, a word of the minimal length $\ell(w)$
representing $w$, and put
$$T_w:=T_{i_1}\cdots T_{i_\ell}\in H_v(n),$$
the empty product when $w$ is the identity of $S_n$, so that $T_w=1$ for that
element. That $T_w$ is independent of the chosen reduced expression, and that
the elements $T_w$ form an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$, is proved in the
standard-basis theorem below
([[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]); the notation
distinguishes the generator $T_i$ with $1\le i\le n-1$ from $T_w$ for the group
element $w$.

**Specializations.** Let $R$ be a commutative $A$-algebra with structure map
$\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]\to R$, $v\mapsto v_0$, and suppose $v_0\in R^\times$. The
**specialization** of $H_v(n)$ at $v_0$ is the $R$-algebra
$R\otimes_AH_v(n)$; it is presented over $R$ by the images of $T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$
subject to the same relations with $v$ replaced by $v_0$, and we write $H_{v_0}(n)$
for it. Two specializations are used on this page: $v\mapsto1$, where the
quadratic relation becomes $T_i^2=1$ together with the braid and commutation
relations, and $v\mapsto q$, where $q$ is the prime power defining
$\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb F_q)$; the latter specializes the generic algebra to
the Hecke algebra attached to the finite general linear group. The condition
$v_0\in R^\times$ is part of the definition of a specialization and, for a nonzero coefficient ring $R$, excludes $v_0=0$. The zero ring
is allowed: its unique element is a unit and its specialization is the zero algebra.

In the generic type-A Hecke algebra $H_v(n)$ over $A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ with
generators $T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$, the quadratic relations
$(T_i-v)(T_i+1)=0$, the braid relations and the distant commutations, and with
$T_w$ the product of the $T_i$ along a reduced word for $w\in S_n$
([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]):

1. $\{T_w:w\in S_n\}$ is an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$; in particular $H_v(n)$ is
free of rank $n!$ over $A$;
2. for every $w\in S_n$ and every $1\le i\le n-1$,
$$T_wT_i=T_{ws_i}\quad\text{if }\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)+1,\qquad T_wT_i=(v-1)T_w+v\,T_{ws_i}\quad\text{if }\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)-1,$$
where $\ell$ is the inversion length of $S_n$
([[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]); consequently the rule rewrites
every monomial in the generators as an $A$-linear combination of the $T_w$.

No choice principle is used.

For $n\ge2$, the symmetric group $S_n$ has the presentation

$$S_n=\langle s_1,\dots,s_{n-1}\mid s_i^2=1,\ s_is_{i+1}s_i=s_{i+1}s_is_{i+1},\ s_is_j=s_js_i\ (|i-j|>1)\rangle,$$

where, after relabelling the underlying set $n=\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$ as
$\{1,\ldots,n\}$, $s_i$ corresponds to the adjacent transposition
$(i\ i+1)$. For
$n=0,1$, the trivial group has the empty presentation.

In the notation of
[[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]], for every
commutative ring $R$ and every $q\in R^\times$:

1. $M(\lambda)$ is free with basis $\{x_\lambda T_d:d\in D_\lambda\}$;

2. $x_\lambda T_w=q^{\ell(w)}x_\lambda$ and $T_wx_\lambda=q^{\ell(w)}x_\lambda$
for every $w\in S_\lambda$, and $x_\lambda^*=x_\lambda$;

3. if $d\in D_\lambda$, $t=t^\lambda\cdot d$ and $s=t\cdot s_i=t^\lambda\cdot d'$, then
$$x_\lambda T_dT_i=\begin{cases}q\,x_\lambda T_d,&s\text{ is not row standard},\\ x_\lambda T_{d'},&s\text{ is row standard and }\ell(d')>\ell(d),\\ q\,x_\lambda T_{d'}+(q-1)x_\lambda T_d,&s\text{ is row standard and }\ell(d')<\ell(d);\end{cases}$$

4. the basis and the action formulas are compatible with every base change
$R\to R'$ along a ring map sending $q$ to a unit.

No choice principle is used.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $q\in R^\times$, let $\lambda\vdash n$
with conjugate $\mu=\lambda'$, and let $H$, $M(\lambda)=x_\lambda H$,
$P(\lambda)=z_\lambda H$ with $z_\lambda=x_\lambda T_{w_\lambda}y_\mu$, the
permutation form $\beta$ and the DJ form $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$ be as in
[[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]]. Write
$b_r:=x_\lambda T_{d_\lambda(r)}$ for the row-standard $\lambda$-tableaux $r$
(the distinguished basis of $M(\lambda)$) and
$$e_t:=z_\lambda T_{d_\mu(t)}\in P(\lambda)\qquad(t\in\operatorname{Std}(\mu)).$$
For row-standard $\lambda$-tableaux $u,v$ write $u\le v$ when for all
$m,k\ge1$ the first $k$ rows of $u$ contain at most as many labels $\le m$ as
the first $k$ rows of $v$, and let $t'$ be the transpose of $t$, a standard
$\lambda$-tableau. Then:

1. $\{e_t:t\in\operatorname{Std}(\mu)\}$ is an $R$-basis of $P(\lambda)$, so
   $P(\lambda)$ is free of rank $f^\lambda=|\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)|$, and
   the inclusion $P(\lambda)\subseteq M(\lambda)$ splits as a map of
   $R$-modules.

2. For every $t\in\operatorname{Std}(\mu)$ one has, with coefficients
   $a_{r,t}\in R$,
   $$e_t=q^{\ell(d_\mu(t))}\,b_{t'}+\sum_{r<t'}a_{r,t}\,b_r,$$
   where the sum runs over the row-standard $r$ with $r\le t'$, $r\ne t'$; the
   square minor with rows $\{t':t\in\operatorname{Std}(\mu)\}$ is therefore
   triangular with respect to any linear extension of the order $\le$ on
   $\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)$, with diagonal entries
   $q^{\ell(d_\mu(t))}$, all units of $R$.

3. The Gram matrix of the DJ form in the basis $\{e_t\}$ is
   $$B_{tu}=\sum_{r}a_{r,t}a_{r,u}q^{\ell(d_\lambda(r))}\qquad(t,u\in\operatorname{Std}(\mu)),$$
   where $a_{r,t}$ denotes the full coefficient of $b_r$ in $e_t$: it is $q^{\ell(d_\mu(t))}$ for $r=t'$, the displayed lower coefficient for $r<t'$, and zero otherwise. Unit triangularity is a property of the
   embedding, not of the Gram matrix: $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$ may be degenerate.

4. Let $(i,j)$ be a Garnir node of $\mu$, that is, a node of $\mu$ with
   $j\le\mu_{i+1}$, put
   $\alpha=(\mu_1,\dots,\mu_{i-1},j-1,\mu_i+1,\mu_{i+1}-j,\mu_{i+2},\dots)$
   with zero parts deleted and $D:=S_\alpha\cap D_\mu$, and let
   $\theta(T_d)\in H$ be the product of the elements
   $\theta(T_r)=(q-1)-T_r$ over a reduced word of $d$
   ([[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]]). Then
   $$z_\lambda\sum_{d\in D}\theta(T_d)=0\qquad\text{in }P(\lambda).$$
   The coefficients are determined by the finite coset identity of step 2.2 and
   survive every base change; together with the unit minor of clause 2 these
   relations give a finite straightening of the elements $z_\lambda T_w$ to
   the standard basis $\{e_t\}$.

5. Every clause is compatible with the base change
   $A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]\to R$, $v\mapsto q$, with $q\in R^\times$. The proof
   uses no generic semisimplicity, divides by no quantum factorial and uses no
   choice principle.

For every commutative ring $R$, every $q\in R^\times$, and every partition
$\lambda\vdash n$ with row symmetrizer $m_\lambda=x_\lambda$, put
$m_{st}:=T_{d(s)}^*m_\lambda T_{d(t)}$ for standard $\lambda$-tableaux $s,t$,
where $d(t)\in D_\lambda$ is the element with $t^\lambda\cdot d(t)=t$. Then:

1. $\{m_{st}:\lambda\vdash n,\ s,t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$ is an
$R$-basis of $H$ (the **Murphy basis**), and $m_{st}^*=m_{ts}$.

2. The $R$-spans $I^{\unrhd\lambda}$ of $\{m_{uv}:\mu\unrhd\lambda\}$ and
$I^{\rhd\lambda}$ of $\{m_{uv}:\mu\rhd\lambda\}$ are two-sided ideals of $H$
(dominance order), and $I^{\unrhd\lambda}/I^{\rhd\lambda}$ is free with basis
the classes of $\{m_{st}:s,t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$.

3. The **Murphy cell module**
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda):=M(\lambda)/(M(\lambda)\cap I^{\rhd\lambda})$ is free
with basis $\{m_t:=x_\lambda T_{d(t)}+I^{\rhd\lambda}:t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$
and satisfies the **cell law**: for $h\in H$ and standard $s,t$,
$$m_{st}h\equiv\sum_{v\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)}r_v\,m_{sv}\pmod{I^{\rhd\lambda}},\qquad r_v\in R,$$
with coefficients $r_v$ independent of $s$.

4. There is a unique $R$-bilinear **Murphy form** $G_\lambda$ on
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ with
$m_{us}m_{tv}\equiv G_\lambda(m_s,m_t)m_{uv}\pmod{I^{\rhd\lambda}}$; it is
symmetric, associative in the sense
$G_\lambda(m_sh,m_t)=G_\lambda(m_s,m_th^*)$, and its radical is a submodule of
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$.

5. The basis, the ideals, the cell law and the form are compatible with every
base change.

The proof also supplies the auxiliary identities used by the comparison:
$\tau(T_w)=\delta_{w,1}$ defines a trace with

derivations.claim: **The group algebra over every coefficient ring.** Let $R$ be any commutative ring and specialize at $q=1$. The Hecke relations become $T_i^2=1$, braid and distant commutation. The Coxeter presentation in [F5] therefore gives the homomorphism $H_{R,1}(S_n)\to R[S_n]$ carrying $T_i$ to $s_i$. A reduced word shows that it carries every $T_w$ to $w$. These are bases of the source and target over $R$, so the map is an isomorphism over $R$, including in positive characteristic and with zero divisors. Equivalently the assignment $s_i\mapsto T_i$ gives its inverse directly from the presentation. No complex-field specialization, dimension comparison over a field or semisimplicity is used.

**Multiplicities and zero quotients.** For a field and unit $q$, the unit form identity in [F1] identifies $D^{\mu}_{\mathrm{DJ}}$ with $(D^{\mu'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta$, including zero quotients. A nonzero cell-form quotient is simple: the cell rank-one action shows that every vector outside its radical generates the cell module, so the radical is its unique maximal submodule. Thus when $D^{\mu'}_{\mathrm M}\ne0$, the module $D^{\mu}_{\mathrm{DJ}}$ is a legitimate simple composition-factor label. Applying the exact twist equivalence in [F2] to a composition series and using [F1] gives $$[P(\lambda):D^{\mu}_{\mathrm{DJ}}]=[C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')^\theta:D^{\mu}_{\mathrm{DJ}}]=[C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda'):(D^{\mu}_{\mathrm{DJ}})^\theta]=[C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda'):D^{\mu'}_{\mathrm M}].$$ This proves clause 2. If a form is identically zero, only its zero form quotient is asserted; no claim is made that the actual module head vanishes.

**The actual polytabloids and the forms.** Give the classical tabloid module the right action $\{t\}\cdot w=\{w^{-1}\cdot t\}=\{t\cdot w\}$. The map $b_d=x_\lambda T_d\mapsto\{t^\lambda\cdot d\}$ sends the distinguished basis to the tabloid basis. It respects the right action: at $q=1$ the row-module multiplication rule is simply the permutation of these cosets, with a same-row transposition acting as $1$. Every diagonal value of $\beta$ becomes $1$, so this is an isometry to the orthonormal tabloid form. The column group of the column-filled tableau $t_\lambda$ is exactly $S_{\lambda'}$, because its columns carry the consecutive row blocks of $\lambda'$. Hence $z_\lambda=x_\lambda w_\lambda\sum_{u\in S_{\lambda'}}\operatorname{sgn}(u)u$ maps to $\sum_u\operatorname{sgn}(u)\{t_\lambda\cdot u\}$, the classical column polytabloid of $t_\lambda$ (replace $u$ by $u^{-1}$ to compare with the left-action formula). Covariance shows $e_t=z_\lambda d_{\lambda'}(t)$ maps to the polytabloid of $t_\lambda\cdot d_{\lambda'}(t)=t'$, the transpose of the standard $\lambda'$-tableau $t$. Thus the actual standard bases correspond bijectively. By the split integral classical basis in [F3] and the split Hecke basis in [F5], this identifies $P(\lambda)$ with $R\otimes_{\mathbb Z}S^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}$ over every $R$, and the restricted DJ form with the restricted tabloid form.

**The exact position of the twist.** At $q=1$, [F2] gives $\theta(T_i)=-T_i$, hence $\theta(w)=\operatorname{sgn}(w)w$. Therefore the right module $P(\lambda)^\theta$ is the sign tensor twist. Applying the involution $\theta$ to [F1] yields $$P(\lambda)^\theta\cong C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda'),$$ without a remaining twist on the Murphy cell. Combining this with the independent same-shape pairing in [F6] gives $P(\lambda)^\theta\cong P(\lambda')^\circ$. Under step 2.1, star dual is the ordinary group contragredient dual, so this is exactly the module identity $S_F^\lambda\otimes\operatorname{sgn}\cong(S_F^{\lambda'})^*$ of [F4] after converting the published left modules to right modules. This asserts the same compatible module dictionary, not an unproved equality of separately normalized explicit maps. In characteristic $2$ the sign becomes trivial at $q=1$; conjugation remains part of the identity.

**Conditional Schur dictionary and conclusion.** Under the stated separate hypothesis on a Schur corner, its images at $\lambda'$ are $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ and $D^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}$. The untwisted Murphy identities from step 3.1 and [F1], valid for arbitrary unit $q$ by involutivity of $\theta$, identify these with $P(\lambda)^\theta$ and $(D^{\lambda}_{\mathrm{DJ}})^\theta$, including the zero quotient. This proves clause 3 without a Schur theorem as a prerequisite. The actual nonzero Schur head and the Hecke cell-form quotient are distinct notions when the corner kills the former. For the empty shape, the generators, forms, twists and all isomorphisms have value $1$. All bases, maps and scalar identities are explicit and use no choice principle.

derivations.claim: **The ordinary module is trivial.** At $q=1$ one has $x_{(3)}=\sum_{w\in S_3}T_w$ and $x_{(3)}T_i=\sum_wT_wT_i=\sum_wT_{ws_i}=x_{(3)}$ for each generator, because right multiplication by $s_i$ permutes the group and every $T_{ws_i}$ is again one of the summed basis elements; with the scalar carried along this reads $x_{(3)}T_i=q\,x_{(3)}=x_{(3)}$ at $q=1$, and $P((3))=x_{(3)}H=\mathbb Q\,x_{(3)}$ is one-dimensional. Its dual is therefore also one-dimensional with trivial action.

**The cell is sign.** At $q=1$ the element $1+T_i$ lies in the higher ideal $I^{\rhd(1^3)}$, because $1+T_1=x_{(2,1)}$ belongs to that two-sided ideal and conjugation by the invertible braid word $T_1T_2$ sends $T_1$ to $T_2$, so $1+T_2$ also belongs to it; hence in the one-dimensional cell $m_0(1+T_i)=0$, that is, $m_0T_i=-m_0$. The cell form value is $1$, and the module is the sign module.

**No untwisted isomorphism.** A right $H$-module isomorphism $f\colon C_{\mathrm M}((1^3))\to P((3))^\circ$ would satisfy $f(mh)=f(m)h$ for every $h$; taking $h=T_i$ and a nonzero $m$ gives $f(-m)=f(m)$ because $C_{\mathrm M}((1^3))$ has $T_i$ acting by $-1$ and $P((3))^\circ$ has $T_i$ acting by $+1$, while $f(-m)=-f(m)$ in characteristic zero, so $-f(m)=f(m)$ forces $f(m)=0$, contradicting injectivity over $\mathbb Q$. Therefore no such isomorphism exists and the untwisted claim is false. The twisted statement is consistent: on $C_{\mathrm M}((1^3))^\theta$ the generator $T_i$ acts by the ordinary action of $\theta(T_i)=-T_i$, that is by $+1$, matching $P((3))$, and the unit is $u_{(3)}=1$ by [F2].

derivations.claim: **Shape (3).** For the one-row shape, $x_{(3)}=\sum_{w\in S_3}T_w$ and pairing $u$ and $us_i$ with $\ell(us_i)=\ell(u)+1$ gives $(T_u+T_{us_i})T_i=q(T_u+T_{us_i})$, hence $x_{(3)}T_i=q\,x_{(3)}$; since $z_{(3)}=x_{(3)}T_{w_{(3)}}y_{(1^3)}=x_{(3)}$ (here $w_{(3)}=1$ and $y_{(1^3)}=1$) the module $P((3))$ is the free rank-one module on $x_{(3)}$ with action $q$. Squaring gives $x_{(3)}^2=\sum_{v,w}T_vT_w=\sum_vT_vx_{(3)}=\bigl(\sum_vq^{\ell(v)}\bigr)x_{(3)}=p_3(q)x_{(3)}$, because the length distribution in $S_3$ is $(1,2,2,1)$ and $1+2q+2q^2+q^3=(1+q)(1+q+q^2)$; hence the Murphy cell has form value $G_{(3)}(c_{(3)},c_{(3)})=p_3(q)$ and action $q$, and $\beta(x_{(3)},x_{(3)})=1$ by [F1].

**Shape (1^3).** For the one-column shape, $x_{(1^3)}=1$ and $P((1^3))=y_{(3)}H$ with $y_{(3)}=\sum_{w\in S_3}(-q)^{-\ell(w)}T_w$. For each pair $u,us_i$ with $\ell(us_i)=\ell(u)+1$, its contribution is $a(T_u-q^{-1}T_{us_i})$, where $a=(-q)^{-\ell(u)}$. The quadratic relation gives $(T_u-q^{-1}T_{us_i})T_i=T_{us_i}-q^{-1}((q-1)T_{us_i}+qT_u)=-(T_u-q^{-1}T_{us_i})$. Summing the pairs gives $y_{(3)}T_i=-y_{(3)}$ for $i=1,2$, the sign representation of the rank-one module. The distinguished basis of $M((1^3))$ is the standard basis and $\beta$ is diagonal with entries $q^{\ell(w)}$, so $\beta(y_{(3)},y_{(3)})=\sum_wq^{-2\ell(w)}q^{\ell(w)}=\sum_wq^{-\ell(w)}=q^{-3}p_3(q)$, the last equality by $w\mapsto w_0w$. Modulo the higher ideal $I^{\rhd(1^3)}$, which contains $1+T_i$ because $1+T_1=x_{(2,1)}$ is a higher Murphy element and conjugation by the invertible braid word $T_1T_2$ sends $T_1$ to $T_2$, placing $1+T_2$ in the same two-sided ideal, the class $c_{(1^3)}$ satisfies $T_i=-1$ and $G_{(1^3)}(c_{(1^3)},c_{(1^3)})=P_{(1^3)}(q)=1$ by [F2].

**The comparison maps.** By [F3] applied to $\lambda=(3)$, where $\lambda'=(1^3)$ and $\ell(w_0(S_{(1^3)}))=\ell(w_{(3)})=0$, the isomorphism $\Phi_{(3)}$ has unit $u_{(3)}=1$ and the identity $G^\theta_{(1^3)}(\Phi_{(3)}x_{(3)},\Phi_{(3)}x_{(3)})=\beta(x_{(3)},x_{(3)})=1$ is consistent because both sides are the value of the respective rank-one forms; explicitly $\Phi_{(3)}(x_{(3)})=c_{(1^3)}$ by [F3]. Applying it to $\lambda=(1^3)$, where $\lambda'=(3)$ and $\ell(w_0(S_{(3)}))=3$, $\ell(w_{(1^3)})=0$, gives $u_{(1^3)}=q^3$, and the identity $G_{(3)}(c_{(3)},c_{(3)})=q^3\,q^{-3}p_3(q)=p_3(q)$ is consistent; explicitly $\Phi_{(1^3)}(y_{(3)})=c_{(3)}$. In the target $C_{\mathrm M}((1^3))^\theta$ the generator acts by the ordinary action of $\theta(T_i)=(q-1)-T_i$, hence by $(q-1)-(-1)=q$ for every unit parameter; at $q=1$ this is $\theta(T_i)=-T_i$ and scalar $+1$; in the target $C_{\mathrm M}((3))^\theta$ it acts by the ordinary action of $(q-1)-T_i$ on the class acting by $q$, hence by $(q-1)-q=-1$; these match the source actions $q$ on $P((3))$ and $-1$ on $P((1^3))$ computed in steps 1.1 and 1.2.

**Specialization and conclusion.** At $q=1$ over $\mathbb Q$ the four form values become $1$, $1^{-3}p_3(1)=6$, $6$ and $1$, and $\theta$ is the sign automorphism exchanging the trivial and sign modules, in agreement with [F4]; the module actions match as in step 2.1. Every displayed identity is an identity in $A=\mathbb Z[q^{\pm1}]$ between Laurent polynomials, so all of them specialize along any ring map $A\to R$ with $q\mapsto q\in R^\times$. Only the rank-one computations, the trace-free form evaluations and the comparison theorem were used; no choice principle is used.

Let $n\ge0$ be an integer, with $S_0=\{1\}$ as in
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]. Let $A:=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ be the ring of Laurent polynomials in one
indeterminate $v$ over $\mathbb Z$. For $n\ge2$ the **generic type-A Hecke
algebra** $H_v(n)$ is the associative unital $A$-algebra presented by generators
$T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$ and the relations
$$T_i^2=(v-1)T_i+v\quad(1\le i<n),\qquad T_iT_{i+1}T_i=T_{i+1}T_iT_{i+1}\quad(1\le i\le n-2),\qquad T_iT_j=T_jT_i\quad(1\le i,j<n,\ |i-j|>1),$$
that is, the quotient of the free unital associative $A$-algebra on
$T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$ by the two-sided ideal generated by these relators. The
first relation is written in the **RG-13 quadratic normalization**
$(T_i-v)(T_i+1)=0$, equivalent to the displayed form over $A$. For $n\le1$ there
are no generators and we set $H_v(n):=A$.

**Standard basis elements.** Let $S_n=\operatorname{Sym}(\{1,\dots,n\})$ with
simple transpositions $s_i=(i\ i+1)$
([[def-symmetric-group]]), and let $w\in S_n$ have inversion length $\ell(w)=\ell$
([[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]). Choose a reduced expression
$w=s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_\ell}$, that is, a word of the minimal length $\ell(w)$
representing $w$, and put
$$T_w:=T_{i_1}\cdots T_{i_\ell}\in H_v(n),$$
the empty product when $w$ is the identity of $S_n$, so that $T_w=1$ for that
element. That $T_w$ is independent of the chosen reduced expression, and that
the elements $T_w$ form an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$, is proved in the
standard-basis theorem below
([[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]); the notation
distinguishes the generator $T_i$ with $1\le i\le n-1$ from $T_w$ for the group
element $w$.

**Specializations.** Let $R$ be a commutative $A$-algebra with structure map
$\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]\to R$, $v\mapsto v_0$, and suppose $v_0\in R^\times$. The
**specialization** of $H_v(n)$ at $v_0$ is the $R$-algebra
$R\otimes_AH_v(n)$; it is presented over $R$ by the images of $T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$
subject to the same relations with $v$ replaced by $v_0$, and we write $H_{v_0}(n)$
for it. Two specializations are used on this page: $v\mapsto1$, where the
quadratic relation becomes $T_i^2=1$ together with the braid and commutation
relations, and $v\mapsto q$, where $q$ is the prime power defining
$\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb F_q)$; the latter specializes the generic algebra to
the Hecke algebra attached to the finite general linear group. The condition
$v_0\in R^\times$ is part of the definition of a specialization and, for a nonzero coefficient ring $R$, excludes $v_0=0$. The zero ring
is allowed: its unique element is a unit and its specialization is the zero algebra.

In the notation of
[[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]], for every
commutative ring $R$ and every $q\in R^\times$:

1. $M(\lambda)$ is free with basis $\{x_\lambda T_d:d\in D_\lambda\}$;

2. $x_\lambda T_w=q^{\ell(w)}x_\lambda$ and $T_wx_\lambda=q^{\ell(w)}x_\lambda$
for every $w\in S_\lambda$, and $x_\lambda^*=x_\lambda$;

3. if $d\in D_\lambda$, $t=t^\lambda\cdot d$ and $s=t\cdot s_i=t^\lambda\cdot d'$, then
$$x_\lambda T_dT_i=\begin{cases}q\,x_\lambda T_d,&s\text{ is not row standard},\\ x_\lambda T_{d'},&s\text{ is row standard and }\ell(d')>\ell(d),\\ q\,x_\lambda T_{d'}+(q-1)x_\lambda T_d,&s\text{ is row standard and }\ell(d')<\ell(d);\end{cases}$$

4. the basis and the action formulas are compatible with every base change
$R\to R'$ along a ring map sending $q$ to a unit.

No choice principle is used.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $q\in R^\times$, let $n\ge0$, and let
$H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$ be the type-A Hecke algebra over $R$ with generators
$T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$, quadratic relations $(T_i-q)(T_i+1)=0$, braid and distant
commutation relations, and standard basis $\{T_w:w\in S_n\}$
([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]],
[[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]); here
$\ell(w)$ is the inversion length of $w\in S_n$
([[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]). All modules below are right
modules.

**The star anti-involution.** Let $\sigma\mapsto\sigma^*$ be the unique
$R$-algebra anti-automorphism of $H$ with $T_i^*=T_i$ for every generator: it
exists because reversal of words preserves the ideal of defining relations
(the quadratic and braid relators are fixed, while a distant commutation relator is sent to its negative), so reversal descends from the free algebra to $H$, and it is
unique because the generators generate $H$. On the standard basis
$T_w^*=T_{w^{-1}}$, since reversing a reduced word for $w$ is a reduced word
for $w^{-1}$.

**Tableau conventions.** Write $t\cdot\sigma$ for the right action of $S_n$ on
tableaux defined by $(t\cdot\sigma)(c):=\sigma^{-1}(t(c))$; it is the inverse
of the left action $(\sigma\cdot t)(c)=\sigma(t(c))$ of
[[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]], and it is a right action.
A $\lambda$-tableau is **row standard** when its entries strictly increase
along every row; columns are not constrained. Let $t^\lambda$ be the row-filled
$\lambda$-tableau, whose row $i$ carries
$\lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_{i-1}+1,\dots,\lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_i$ from left
to right, and let $t_\lambda$ be the column-filled $\lambda$-tableau, whose
column $j$ carries consecutive integers downward; equivalently
$t_\lambda(i,j)=t^{\lambda'}(j,i)$, so that $t_\lambda$ is the transpose of
$t^{\lambda'}$ ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]).

**The row subgroup and the coset representatives.** Let $S_\lambda$ be the
**row subgroup** of $\lambda$, the subgroup of $S_n$ preserving every row of
$t^\lambda$; writing
$$B_i:=\{\lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_{i-1}+1,\ \lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_{i-1}+2,\ \dots,\ \lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_i\}$$
for the $i$-th row block of $t^\lambda$, one has
$S_\lambda=S(B_1)\times\cdots\times S(B_k)$, the direct product of the
symmetric groups of the individual row blocks. Let
$$D_\lambda:=\{d\in S_n:t^\lambda\cdot d\text{ is row standard}\}.$$
This is the set of minimal-length right coset representatives of $S_\lambda$ in
$S_n$: every right coset $S_\lambda d$ has exactly one element $d_0$ for which
$t^\lambda\cdot d_0$ is row standard, and it satisfies
$\ell(wd_0)=\ell(w)+\ell(d_0)$ for all $w\in S_\lambda$
([[lem-dj-bridge-row-permutation-module-standard-action]]). Let
$w_\lambda\in S_n$ be the unique element with $t^\lambda\cdot w_\lambda=t_\lambda$;
existence and uniqueness hold because the action of $S_n$ on $\lambda$-tableaux
is free and transitive.

**Generators and modules.** For a partition $\lambda\vdash n$ put
$$x_\lambda:=\sum_{w\in S_\lambda}T_w,\qquad y_\lambda:=\sum_{w\in S_\lambda}(-q)^{-\ell(w)}T_w,\qquad z_\lambda:=x_\lambda T_{w_\lambda}y_{\lambda'},$$
where $\lambda'$ is the conjugate partition of $\lambda$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). The **row
permutation module** is the right ideal $M(\lambda):=x_\lambda H\subseteq H$,
and the **ordinary Dipper-James polytabloid module** is
$P(\lambda):=z_\lambda H\subseteq M(\lambda)$; $z_\lambda$ is its polytabloid
generator.

**The forms.** The **permutation form** is the $R$-bilinear form $\beta$ on
$M(\lambda)$ determined on the distinguished family
$\{x_\lambda T_d:d\in D_\lambda\}$ by
$$\beta(x_\lambda T_d,x_\lambda T_e)=\delta_{d,e}q^{\ell(d)}\qquad(d,e\in D_\lambda),$$
and the **DJ form** is the restriction of $\beta$ to $P(\lambda)$. That family
is an $R$-basis of $M(\lambda)$
([[lem-dj-bridge-row-permutation-module-standard-action]]), so the displayed
values define a unique bilinear form; the family is $\{x_\varnothing\}=\{1\}$
for the empty partition.

**Small cases and base change.** For $\lambda=\varnothing$ set
$x_\varnothing=y_\varnothing=z_\varnothing=1$, so that
$M(\varnothing)=P(\varnothing)=R$ and $\beta$ is the standard form; for
$n=0,1$ there are no generators and $H=R$. Every base change
$A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]\to R$, $v\mapsto q$, with $q\in R^\times$, produces all
objects above over $R$ by the same formulas; the suppliers of this page prove
that the distinguished families and the form are compatible with such base
change. No choice principle is used.

In the notation of
[[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]], for every
commutative ring $R$ and every $q\in R^\times$:

1. $M(\lambda)$ is free with basis $\{x_\lambda T_d:d\in D_\lambda\}$;

2. $x_\lambda T_w=q^{\ell(w)}x_\lambda$ and $T_wx_\lambda=q^{\ell(w)}x_\lambda$
for every $w\in S_\lambda$, and $x_\lambda^*=x_\lambda$;

3. if $d\in D_\lambda$, $t=t^\lambda\cdot d$ and $s=t\cdot s_i=t^\lambda\cdot d'$, then
$$x_\lambda T_dT_i=\begin{cases}q\,x_\lambda T_d,&s\text{ is not row standard},\\ x_\lambda T_{d'},&s\text{ is row standard and }\ell(d')>\ell(d),\\ q\,x_\lambda T_{d'}+(q-1)x_\lambda T_d,&s\text{ is row standard and }\ell(d')<\ell(d);\end{cases}$$

4. the basis and the action formulas are compatible with every base change
$R\to R'$ along a ring map sending $q$ to a unit.

No choice principle is used.

For every commutative ring $R$, every $q\in R^\times$, and every partition
$\lambda\vdash n$ with row symmetrizer $m_\lambda=x_\lambda$, put
$m_{st}:=T_{d(s)}^*m_\lambda T_{d(t)}$ for standard $\lambda$-tableaux $s,t$,
where $d(t)\in D_\lambda$ is the element with $t^\lambda\cdot d(t)=t$. Then:

1. $\{m_{st}:\lambda\vdash n,\ s,t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$ is an
$R$-basis of $H$ (the **Murphy basis**), and $m_{st}^*=m_{ts}$.

2. The $R$-spans $I^{\unrhd\lambda}$ of $\{m_{uv}:\mu\unrhd\lambda\}$ and
$I^{\rhd\lambda}$ of $\{m_{uv}:\mu\rhd\lambda\}$ are two-sided ideals of $H$
(dominance order), and $I^{\unrhd\lambda}/I^{\rhd\lambda}$ is free with basis
the classes of $\{m_{st}:s,t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$.

3. The **Murphy cell module**
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda):=M(\lambda)/(M(\lambda)\cap I^{\rhd\lambda})$ is free
with basis $\{m_t:=x_\lambda T_{d(t)}+I^{\rhd\lambda}:t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$
and satisfies the **cell law**: for $h\in H$ and standard $s,t$,
$$m_{st}h\equiv\sum_{v\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)}r_v\,m_{sv}\pmod{I^{\rhd\lambda}},\qquad r_v\in R,$$
with coefficients $r_v$ independent of $s$.

4. There is a unique $R$-bilinear **Murphy form** $G_\lambda$ on
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ with
$m_{us}m_{tv}\equiv G_\lambda(m_s,m_t)m_{uv}\pmod{I^{\rhd\lambda}}$; it is
symmetric, associative in the sense
$G_\lambda(m_sh,m_t)=G_\lambda(m_s,m_th^*)$, and its radical is a submodule of
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$.

5. The basis, the ideals, the cell law and the form are compatible with every
base change.

The proof also supplies the auxiliary identities used by the comparison:
$\tau(T_w)=\delta_{w,1}$ defines a trace with
$\tau(T_u^*T_v)=\delta_{u,v}q^{\ell(u)}$ (step 1.3); for a composition
$\alpha$ and the partition $\beta$ obtained by sorting its parts,
$x_\alpha=T_dx_\beta T_d^{-1}$ with a block-reordering permutation $d$
(step 2.2); and for the Garnir composition $\alpha$ at a node of $\rho$,
$x_\rho\sum_{d\in S_\alpha\cap D_\rho}T_d
=\sum_{v\in S_\rho\cap D_\alpha}T_v^*x_\alpha$ (step 2.3).
The block-reordering and Garnir data are specified in those steps.

In particular $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ is finite free of rank
$f^\lambda=|\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)|$. No choice principle is used.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^\times$ and $\lambda\vdash n$, and write $\mu=\lambda'$, $L=\ell(w_\lambda)$ and $N=\ell(w_0(S_{\lambda'}))$. Let $P(\lambda)=z_\lambda H$ with its DJ form $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$, the cell module $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ with its Murphy form $G_{\lambda'}$, and the sign automorphism $\theta$ be as in [[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]], [[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]] and [[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]], and let $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')^\theta$ be the $\theta$-twisted cell module of [[lem-dj-bridge-theta-transport-of-the-cellular-structure]]. Then:

1. There is a base-change compatible isomorphism of right $H$-modules $$\Phi_\lambda\colon P(\lambda)\longrightarrow C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')^\theta,\qquad \Phi_\lambda(z_\lambda)=m_0,\quad \Phi_\lambda(z_\lambda h)=m_0\theta(h)\ \ (h\in H),$$ where $m_0$ is the class of $x_{\lambda'}$ in $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ and the right side is computed with the ordinary action on $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ and read in the twist; in particular $\Phi_\lambda(e_t)=m_0\theta(T_{d_{\lambda'}(t)})$ for $t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda')$. For a class $m\in C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ and any lift $\widetilde m\in M(\lambda')$, the inverse is $\Phi_\lambda^{-1}(m)=q^{-N}x_\lambda T_{w_\lambda}\theta(\widetilde m)$, independently of the chosen lift.

2. With $G_{\lambda'}^\theta$ the transported form of [[lem-dj-bridge-theta-transport-of-the-cellular-structure]] and $u_\lambda(q):=q^{\ell(w_0(S_{\lambda'}))-\ell(w_\lambda)}\in A^\times$, $$G_{\lambda'}^\theta(\Phi_\lambda x,\Phi_\lambda y)=u_\lambda(q)\,\beta_{P(\lambda)}(x,y)\qquad(x,y\in P(\lambda)),$$ over every commutative $R$ with $q\in R^\times$. No unnamed scalar and no potentially vanishing scalar occurs: $u_\lambda$ is the explicit unit $q^{N-L}$ in the fixed normalizations of this page.

3. Consequently $\Phi_\lambda$ maps the radical of $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$ onto the radical of $G_{\lambda'}^\theta$, the induced map between the quotients is an isomorphism, with the corresponding cell-form quotients $D^{\lambda}_{\mathrm{DJ}}\cong(D^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta$, including the zero-quotient case. Over a field, when the quotients are nonzero they are the simple heads; when the forms are identically zero, the displayed quotients are zero and no assertion about the actual module heads is made. Over a PID with a chosen prime, the unit-scaled form identity preserves all divisibility submodules and their reductions. One also obtains $P(\lambda')\cong P(\lambda)^{\circ,\theta}$ with the exact position of the dual and the twist, separating same-shape duality from conjugate-sign transport. No choice principle is used.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^\times$ and $\lambda\vdash n$, and let $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ with its basis $\{m_t\}$, $P(\lambda)=z_\lambda H$, the permutation form $\beta$ on $M(\lambda)$ and the DJ form on $P(\lambda)$ be as in [[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]], [[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]] and [[lem-dj-bridge-integral-murphy-and-polytabloid-straightening]]. Then:

1. Setting $B_\lambda(m_s,p):=\beta(x_\lambda T_{d_\lambda(s)},p)$ for $s\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)$ and $p\in P(\lambda)$ defines an explicit $R$-bilinear pairing $B_\lambda\colon C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)\times P(\lambda)\to R$ that is $H$-balanced, $B_\lambda(mh,p)=B_\lambda(m,ph^*)$, and whose adjoint $c\mapsto B_\lambda(c,-)$ is an isomorphism of right $H$-modules $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)\to P(\lambda)^\circ$ onto the star-contragredient module of [[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]]. No nondegeneracy of the DJ form $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$ is required.

2. Equivalently, the kernel of the quotient map $M(\lambda)\to C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ is the orthogonal complement $P(\lambda)^\perp=\{a\in M(\lambda):\beta(a,p)=0\text{ for all }p\in P(\lambda)\}$, namely $M(\lambda)\cap I^{\rhd\lambda}$; the pairing matrices in the bases $\{m_s\}$ and $\{e_t\}$ have entries $B_\lambda(m_s,e_t)=q^{\ell(d_\lambda(s))}a_{d_\lambda(s),t}$ with $e_t=\sum_d a_{d,t}b_d$, and determinant a unit of $A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$. Their inverses are finite tableau formulas given by the adjugate divided by this unit.

3. All statements are compatible with every base change $A\to R$, $v\mapsto q$; the construction uses no generic semisimplicity, no nondegeneracy of $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$ and no choice principle.

derivations.claim: **Row module.** From [F1], $b_0T_1=xT_1=qx=q\,b_0$, $b_1T_1=xT_2T_1=b_2$ and $b_2T_1=xT_2T_1^2=xT_2((q-1)T_1+q)=(q-1)b_2+q\,b_1$; also $b_0T_2=b_1$, $b_1T_2=xT_2^2=x((q-1)T_2+q)=(q-1)b_1+q\,b_0$ and $b_2T_2=xT_2T_1T_2=xT_1T_2T_1=q\,xT_2T_1=q\,b_2$, using the braid relation. In the basis $(b_0,b_1,b_2)$ with coordinate row vectors these are exactly the matrices $R_1$ and $R_2$ of the statement, and $\beta(b_i,b_i)=q^{i}$ by [F2] because $\ell(1)=0$, $\ell(s_2)=1$, $\ell(s_2s_1)=2$.

**Polytabloids and their form.** Since $z_\lambda=xT_2(1-q^{-1}T_1)$ by [F4] and $y_{\lambda'}=1-q^{-1}T_1$, the displayed expressions $p_0=b_1-q^{-1}b_2$ and $p_1=zT_2=b_1T_2-q^{-1}b_2T_2=qb_0+(q-1)b_1-b_2$ follow from step 1.1. Their coordinates on $(b_0,b_2)$ give the matrix $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&-q^{-1}\\q&-1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ with determinant $q\cdot q^{-1}=1$, a unit over every $R$; hence the two polytabloids span a free rank-two split submodule. The row action gives $p_0T_1=-p_0$, $p_1T_1=-q^2p_0+qp_1$, $p_0T_2=p_1$ and $p_1T_2=qp_0+(q-1)p_1$. Thus their span is stable, has precisely the displayed matrices $P_1,P_2$, and equals $zH$ because it contains $z=p_0$ and $zT_2=p_1$. Weighted inner products against the diagonal form of [F2] give $B=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}q+1&q^2\\q^2&q^3+q\end{smallmatrix}\right)$: explicitly $B_{00}=q+q^{-2}\cdot q^2=q+1$, $B_{01}=q(q-1)+(-q^{-1})(-1)q^2=q(q-1)+q=q^2$, and $B_{11}=q^2+(q-1)^2q+q^2=q^3+q$. Its determinant is $q(q^2+q+1)$.

**The Murphy quotient.** In $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ the higher vector $x_{(3)}=b_0+b_1+b_2$ vanishes by [F3], so $b_2=-c_0-c_1$ and $c_1=xT_2=b_1$. Then $c_0T_1=qx=q\,c_0$ and $c_1T_1=b_2=-c_0-c_1$, giving $M_1$; also $c_0T_2=c_1$ and $c_1T_2=(q-1)b_1+qb_0=(q-1)c_1+qc_0$, giving $M_2$. The defining products of [F3] give $x^2=(q+1)x$ and $xT_2x=b_1+b_2=x_{(3)}-x\equiv-x$. Also $xT_2^2x=(q-1)xT_2x+qx^2\equiv(q^2+1)x$. Reading the coefficient of $m_{t_0t_0}=x$ therefore gives $G(c_0,c_0)=q+1$, $G(c_0,c_1)=-1$ and $G(c_1,c_1)=q^2+1$; equivalently $G=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}q+1&-1\\-1&q^2+1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ with determinant $q^3+q^2+q$.

**Comparison, cross-pairing and specializations.** The comparison theorem of [F4] gives $\Phi(z)=c_0$, hence $\Phi(p_1)=\Phi(zT_2)=c_0\theta(T_2)=(q-1)c_0-c_1$ and $A=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\q-1&-1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$; direct matrix multiplication verifies $P_iA=A((q-1)I-M_i)$ for $i=1,2$ and $AGA^{\mathsf T}=B$, the latter being the form identity with the unit $u_\lambda=1$. The cross-pairing entries $B_\lambda(c_s,p_t)=\beta(b_{d(s)},p_t)$ on the standard bases give $Q=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&q\\q&q(q-1)\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ with $\det Q=-q^2\in A^\times$, so the pairing is perfect as in [F4]. The two Gram determinants agree with $q(1+q+q^2)$. At $q=-1$ in characteristic zero, $B=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&-2\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ and $G=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&-1\\-1&2\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ have determinant $-1$, although $[2]_q=1+q=0$; at $q=1$ in characteristic $2$, both reduce to $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ with determinant $1$, hence with zero radical. All identities are Laurent-polynomial identities, so they specialize to every $R$; no choice principle is used.
